I'm glad I didn't pay anything for this book. It jumped from one action scene to the next, without even the slightest explanation of what was going on, meaning I have less idea of what this book is about than before I actually read it. I didn't like how people were portrayed either. It's like the only people in the world were her, her brother (who buggers off after just one scene together) and the two hot guys who of course she loves after falling on hopelessly in love after like a day, with barely any communication. On that note, after 3,000 years surely someone should know better than to abandon everything for some girl they've only just met?? . This book makes Disney characters look like they think their relationships out thoroughly. Oh, and I forgot this one, probably because it was made to seem so unimportant, but her mum tells her she's not really her mother, then this is only actually mentioned once after, like it was such a minor detail. No matter how bad their relationship was, wouldn't you feel weird finding out the person who raised you wasn't actually your mother? She didn't even seem interested in who her mother was. It was like the author decided to bring in a new storyline then got bored of it after about 2 minutes but forgot to take it out. There are a couple of good points. I did like Jonah, although I'm disappointed that his part just tapers off. There's also the fact that the book was short, so the torture was over pretty quickly.

This final installment of the Millennium Series reveals the intrigue that was developed in the previous two books. This book moves slower than the second book partly because Lisbeth is in the hospital because of an attempt to seek revenge on her father that backfired. The kick-ass heroine has little action time in this book until the very cliff-hanger ending. The story however is more of a character study of Lisbeth where in the first time her life her freedom is dependent upon trusting other people. This is not an easy thing for her to do. It is a shame that this series hasn't had an opportunity to be expanded. There is plenty of great material to build on. There is even a twin sister to Lisbeth! All in all, this is unique and great story in the mystery and thriller type books.

I was very pleased to see a drastic decrease in the over-usage of random ellipsis. Without the punctuation errors, Armentrout's novels read like a teenage girl excitedly reciting a story to her friends. Which is a good thing! It really helped the book flow from sentence to chapter all the way to the end. There is something addicting about the way she writes, and I enjoy it. On the downside, I should have seen the dreaded YA love triangle coming.

This book started out so well. I was captivated from the first page. I just had to find out more, my thoughts went like this: "why is this child trapped in the attic" and "I like Julia, she seems troubled but kind, I can't wait to see her character development". Then we come to the last hundred pages of the novel and my thoughts at this point are "who the f*** does that?" And "why wasn't Julia's story more developed" finally "no parent who wanted a child that badly would do something so awful". I am also very disappointed that the ending felt unfinished. Julia is never good no to know how much her mother and father loved her and cared for her. I'm sorry to say that I wouldn't recommend this book. The first half was great, then the novel seemed to drag on while just about every character became a more terrible person than they were in the chapter before.

What a HUGE letdown. I liked Cinder a lot, so it's probably my fault for having high expectations for Scarlet. I read both books right after each other in a span of 11 hours (too excited. Don't judge), so you could probably trust me when I say that Cinder is the better book. Scarlet is just okay. A little meh on the side, and you may feel a flash of anger every time one of the characters makes stupid decisions. But you know, reading is so subjective. I just really hope Cress will be sooooo much better than this. And omg, you should have seen my face when I read the last bit about Wolf swearing on his eternal devotion to Scarlet after less than a week of meeting each other. It was so Twilight-ish! Gag!

Oh my god, okay, where to begin WHY I have this book one star. For starters, I give it one star for one reason: I finished it. That's it. It was drivel, but I finished it. Sam and Grace are not likeable characters. They are the same person with a different name. The author tried at several points to make Sam a 'deep' character. Well, the songs suck. They were cheesy. Grace had no depth - her character was shallow, there was no iceberg effect here. No 'read between the lines' or anything like that. Plain old Grace, whose only interesting feature was an interest in wolves. Hey, we all have an interest in animals, whether we like them or not. I squeal whenever I see a panda. However, I can't say that I count down the months until I go to the zoo and see a panda. Grace, however, has made her life's meaning to look at a wolf that didn't kill her once. I read this book at 14, during my Twilight phase. That should tell you something about my literary preferences back then! Yet, I still didn't like it. A year or so ago, at 16, I attempted to read it again. No such luck. My then 14 year old sister read it and thought the same as me. Imagine two mid-teen girls shuddering in a bookstore. That was us when we saw that the author had a second series. If you happen to read this Maggie, your writing is good. You don't bombard us with big, unnecessary words to seem smarter or to make a sure-fire spot in the Classics section 50 years from now. However, character development is what really let you down here.

Nova Ren Suma's 17 & GONE was such a unique read. After growing interested in a missing person's case (a seventeen-year-old girl who vanished from a nearby summer camp), Lauren begins having visions of more missing girls. The deeper she digs for clues, the more convoluted the truth becomes. Why are the girls speaking to her? Can she help them? Who is still alive, and...Could Lauren be next? First and foremost, Nova's writing is gorgeous. This book goes down like honey, and the tone is both serene and spine-tingling eerie at once. Lauren's visions are shockingly well realized, and entirely compelling. (While the story unfolds at a steady but rather slow clip, I eagerly kept turning pages.) More than anything, I love an unreliable narrator, and 17 & GONE gives us just that. Lauren is a reliable until she's not, and suddenly the reader is left wondering what is real, what is a lie, what is supernatural, and what is something else. I can't say much else without risking spoilers, but I thought the subject matter was handled deftly, and the final reveal and conclusion, powerful. Originally posted here.

Love Me in the Dark by Mia Asher is a standalone romance that borders on a love-triangle trope without ever fully stepping into that darkness. It is beautifully written to showcase the depth of conflict between the lead married female, Valentina, her apathetic husband, William, and the successful Parisian artist, Sebastien. Valentina thought she had it all. The happy marriage, the doting husband, the comfortable life. When she catches her husband, on their anniversary, cheating on her, the next year is spent dissecting their years together and trying to move past this heartbreaking event. When he offers to get away with her and go to Paris for some much needed time together she finally thinks things are on the mend and is willing to open up and maybe let him back into her heart. When he gets held up by meetings and sends her on ahead then never shows she is left to discover her true self, alone, in Paris. Sebastien is a troubled man who has suffered much loss in his life. He is a successful, renowned and wealthy artist who hasn't opened himself up to love in years. When he meets Valentina, by coincidence, at a gallery party, the attraction and intrigue is instantaneous for him. He wants more but they go their separate ways only to have fate play it's hand and have Valentina staying in his same apartment building. They build a solid friendship through the months she stays there all the while knowing that a reckoning is coming in the way of William and none of them will like it. Magical. I loved every word. I have laid out the gist of the story above without letting any of the sordid details loose and it is the sordid details, Sebastien's past, William's own nasty secrets, and Valentina's true desires, that make this story so amazing. Enjoy!

from pagetrotter.blogspot.com You guuuuuuuys!!!!! *happy dancing* What's one of my favorite things? Banter. It's awesome, funny banter! The Curse Keepers has it in spades! Gah, what can I say about this? First, thanks Amber Lynn Natusch for the recommendation because she pointed me in this direction and I'm so glad she did! I've been on an Urban Fantasy/Para-Romance kick lately and I've not been disappointed yet! Let me tell you why I freaking LOVE this book. Ellie and Collin are fated in a prophecy to be each other's counterpart. What does this mean? Are they soul mates? Enemies? Well, it's more like co-workers. Yes, there is chemistry, but there is no insta-love here! In fact, it's more like insta-I wanna slap your face. Seriously, Collin is kind of an ass hole and Ellie is a little bit of a pain in the ass. I love their relationship. I love that they are constantly giving each other shit and call each other out. Gah, love-hate relationships are some of my favorite romances. I'm sick, I know this. What else do I love? Well, my degree is in History and while my focus was on Russian and Eastern European medieval history (sounds fascinating and oddly specific right? Right!) I love ALL history! This book revolves around the story of the first colony-Roanoke! I love the lore that the author creates, I love the Native American elements she weaves so seamlessly into it. For over 300 pages, I soared through this book quickly. It's fast paced and action packed! I was nail biting one second and laughing out loud the next. And ladies, prepare for Collin to make you swoon in a whole different way. He's a dick, but he's so funny and unapologetic. He's loyal and so different from most of the heroes out there. No disposal income for this guy which oddly was one of the things I liked about him? He's fierce and protective of those he loves. Ellie is a trooper. That's really the first word that comes to mind. She's got it tough financially. Her life is pretty stagnant, but she comes out swinging when life throws shit her way and I love her spunk. I also love that she doesn't let anyone walk all over her. She doesn't give Collin an inch and it's awesome! This is book one in a series! I really enjoy this author so after you've checked out this book, why don't you check out some of her other stuff? She has an awesome contemporary series out that I really enjoy, the Off the Subject series.

DNF at 200 pages I know this book is incredibly loved, and proclaimed a sci-fi classic that propelled many people into the genre, but I was bored out of my mind. While reading this I felt that I didn't know what was going on half the time, especially during the "battles." I found the author's attempt to orient the reader during the battle situations only left me more confused. Not only that, but I didn't care. I felt nothing towards any of the characters, leaving a disconnect, furthering my boredom while reading. Ender was an unrealistic portal of a six year old. I'm sorry, I understand that he is "special", and that they have "plans for him", but the thoughts he was having did not follow the thought process of a six year old, no matter their IQ. I found it off-putting to read, and left me picturing Ender as a teenager, instead of someone that is actually significantly younger. This is the fifth book I have read by James and the third one in her series based on fairy tales. I have enjoyed them all. Her characters are entertaining, there is always humorous aspects to the story, I have lots of fun with her plotting and of course, it all works out in the end. I especially enjoyed her take on Cinderella in this book. As I have said many times before, romances are my escapist entertainment. Now that I can get romance novels on my kindle, I never have to worry about being without a chance to indulge and I can be sure that James' tales will always take me away from my day to day drudgery.

They say the third time is the charm, and that certainly is the case for K.A. Tucker's Ten Tiny Breaths series. While I enjoyed Ten Tiny Breaths, I thought it followed the standard New Adult Trauma Victim Plot pretty closely, and One Tiny Lie was mostly about Livie learning to party like a college girl. It also had that pesky cheating triangle (Take that with a grain of salt, as many people didn't see that book as negatively as I did). Four Seconds to Lose is book three in the companion series, and the story follows club owner Cain and his new hire Charlie. For me, it is by far the best of the three. Four Seconds to Lose is much more mature and serious than Kacey and Livie's books, and it felt like the story crossed the line into being an "Adult Contemporary" as opposed to a "New Adult". Even though Charlie is the same age as Livie, she and Cain are dealing with much bigger issues than themselves, and the story is less focused on self discovery. And, as much as people love him, I think the absence of wacky Dr. Strayner, made this book better. He started to become too much of a powerful fix all character, and his unconventional methods never rang true to me. I was already intrigued by Cain after glimpsing him in the previous two novels, and boy did I fall hard for him in this book. But it didn't take me long to sympathize with Charlie as well. It's interesting because she is keeping some big secrets from him throughout most of the story, and that frustrated me at times. However, she was deep in a dangerous situation that had no good out, and I could understand her fear over it. I also liked how the romance was paced. Although Cain and Charlie are instantly attracted to each other, it takes time for anything to happen between them. All that building tension was pretty delicious. When I read the description of this book, I was a little worried. Cain owns a strip club through which he tries to help women escape the sex business. WHAT? In Cain's mind, a strip club attracts women who are already using their bodies to make money, and he uses that avenue to help the women who work with him. He keeps his business clean, legal and drug free, and works hard to encourage the girls to get out of the industry and away from bad relationships by encouraging therapy and education. Cain has a very strict policy of no relationships with his staff, which he's been able to keep easily, until Charlie shows up at his door. Despite all of his explanations, Cain's reasoning for running a strip club still sounded pretty flimsy to me. Before I started this book, I was convinced that I'd never buy his excuses. But the thing is, I did, especially because Cain also struggles with these same questions, and wonders if he's actually helping or enabling these women. It is clear that owning the club is wearing on him. I was really surprised that despite somewhat flawed logic, I bought his perspective, and could see good in what he was doing. Four Seconds to Lose can be read as a standalone, but I did appreciate having a background on Cain from reading Kacey's story in Ten Tiny Breaths. The time frame for the plot of One Tiny Lie overlaps with this one and is not relevant to this story. Despite my hesitation about the previous books, this series has continued to hold my interest, and I finally truly get what everyone's talking about with these books. I can't wait for the next installment, Five Ways to Fall, which is about Ben (though it is starting to bother me that Four Seconds to Lose is book three and Five Ways to Fall is book four. We need to add another before them for them to add up correctly! Love Triangle Factor: None Cliffhanger Scale: Low/none. Third in companion series.

I don't know what book everyone else read, but this is not a 5-star book by any scale that I would use. The writing is mediocre, the characters are frustrating (Devon, Ezra) or flat (Cas, Devon's parents) or can't seem to decide how old they are (Foster, Marabelle), and the plotting was strange. Every scene felt like it was cut short, like they ended in places that didn't make sense for them to end. The whole book felt this way, actually. I didn't get enough of anything from this book, and I can't decide if that's because it tried to do too much or it didn't try to do enough. Like, we've got the whole Foster-moving-in-with-Devon thing. Okay, fine. Go with that. Show her struggle to adapt to having a new family member around all the time; show the growth in her relationship with Foster. Instead, what I saw was Devon complaining for no apparent reason that this kid came to live with them, not explaining what was really going on with his mom (really. the whole book goes by and you can't say the word "depression," or whatever it was that sent her into rehab (or wherever she was, since I'm pretty sure the word "rehab" is never said either)? ), and then becoming an overprotective "big sister" the moment something mildly bad happens to him. Basically what I wanted in the Devon/Foster relationship was for the author to dig deeper. The focus on everything that happens to Foster takes away from Devon's involvement in the action--nothing ever really happens to her, and for that reason she doesn't have a ton of character development, either. The book opens with her being told that her personal essay for a college application wasn't good enough, but never comes back to it. She never really starts to care about college; we don't see her apply at all, and the extracurricular that she halfheartedly signs up for comes way too easily--literally all she has to do is hold a camera bag, and she even complains about that. She gets a byline in the school newspaper just for emailing with the guy who eventually becomes her love interest. Woe is Devon, it's a hard knock life. The romance takes a backseat and relies on the all-too-convenient "all of our conflict comes from lack of communication" trope, so I don't have a lot to say about it. I took a break from reading to text my friend and tell her how tired I am of contemporary romance authors defaulting to miscommunication as a source of tension. [Don't get me wrong, some books do it well--like Anna and the French Kiss--and some contemporary authors continually succeed at avoiding it, like Morgan Matson and Sarah Ockler. But alas, those few authors can't come out with dozens of books a year and sometimes I have to settle for stuff like this.] The Jane Austen stuff is the book's main draw and frankly, I felt like it didn't need to be there. Devon says the one criticism she has of "Jane's" books are that the couple-finally-gets-together scenes are too short and there's not enough kissing, AND THEN SHE GIVES US EVEN LESS OF THAT EXACT THING. Everyone at least remembers the scene in Pride & Prejudice when Darcy confesses his love and all that jazz, but I finished First & Then two days ago and I could not even tell you if Devon and Ezra kissed at the end. I assume they did, but I legitimately don't remember. Here are the three bullet points that I did like about this book: -it was funny, and I liked Devon's voice -I appreciate that the author at least tried to emphasize female friendship, even if it was only once in the whole book -I loved Jordan. Loved him. Why wasn't he the love interest? Ezra was okay, but Jordan was like sunshine on the page. This is not a book I'd recommend if you're looking for a cute, swoony contemporary romance, because there barely is a romance. It's not a book I'd recommend if you want a moving family story, because the family situation is neither explained well nor very nuanced, and I was not moved. If you want a fast read with a funny but irritating narrator, well then go ahead and grab a copy of First & Then.

I liked but didn't love this book. I couldn't really relate to the main character but I did enjoy quite of a few of the more side characters. And the ending was fairly obvious. Not my favorite book I've read recently but something I did enjoy reading.

"Emmy and Oliver" is not a complicated book. (It is, however, the second book I've read this year with a "X Girl's Name and Oliver" title. It's much better than than the first, "Althea and Oliver".) Boy meets girl (when, they're, like, infants.) Boy and girl become best friends, growing up and in like with each other. Boy gets kidnapped by his father at age seven, changing everyone's lives forever. Boy returns home ten years later. Okay, yeah, it might seem a little complicated. But honestly, it wasn't. "Emmy and Oliver" could have been an incredibly heavy, downcast book. Yet it managed to balance slice-of-life best-friends-fallig-in-love romance with a very dramatic angle involving kidnapping and how it affects not only the kidnapee but everyone touched by him. Much of the novel does deal with the fallout of Oliver's kidnapping--his trauma, the changes in his family, the overprotectiveness it triggers in Emmy's parents. Yet never did I feel like Oliver's kidnapping overshadowed his relationship with Emmy, which is, of course, the heart of the novel. Really, I think Benway approached the subject in an unexpected manner. I'd thought a lot about Oliver's experience prior to reading the book. But I didn't--I doubt that people in general--consider the effect it would have on Emmy's home life. As Oliver's best friend and neighbor, she was closer to him than most, her family linked to his. So it makes perfect sense that her parents would become insanely sheltering and oppressive, but... I hadn't imagiend it. (That being said, I do think that Emmy's parents came off as rather thinly-drawn. I know the point was that their behavior was irrational, but it just didn't come together for me all the time.) Sometimes, I felt like the book veered away from what Oliver was going through a little TOO much. It's not a hugely impactful novel; more of a romance than a character piece of exploration of an "event". But that was okay. It was a good read, and Oliver and Emmy's relationship was both cute and refreshing. Refreshing in that it had very little "stupid conflict" that didn't make sense. To be honest, the book could have used a little MORE conflict. But that may be because I'm a horrid drama queen. What more can I say? It was cute, it was fluffy, I really liked it.

Wow. Just wow. It's been days since I read this, and I'm still not sure how to do review this properly, because I still haven't processed it. I absolutely loved it. It started out a bit slow, but the pace just got faster throughout, and I have to say, the slow beginning actually added to the plot, to the tension and excitement. Sal felt realistic and relatable, and I loved to see how they grew through the book, and I also loved the romance. It didn't take any attention from the action or the plot - in fact, it only added to the tension. I loved reading about Sal! Despite Mask of Shadows being a High Fantasy, Sal felt very realistic. It was easy to relate to them and it was interesting to read about them. Sal also grew a lot through the book, and it was amazing to follow their journey. And I have to say something about the diversity in this book. Way too often in Fantasy, I feel like there isn't any diversity, and if there is, it feels a bit like it's there just for the sake of it being there. It's the complete opposite with Mask of Shadows, it feels completely natural and it's so important. The romance was really sweet and so intense! I really liked how the author portrayed the romance between Sal and Elise, it progressed slowly through the whole book, which made it feel realistic. Also, I have to say they are simply too cute together! I shipped them from the moment Sal robbed her, which is definitely a first for me. I just really love how they interact with each other, from the moment they first met - not to mention the tension that is there from the beginning. This is how romance should be portrayed in Fantasy books! The world-building is what dreams are made of! First of all, the author has created such an amazing, unique and utterly interesting world - from the first page, you just have to know more, making it impossible to stop reading, even for just a moment (who cares about school, anyway, I can study after I'm finished). I had no idea what to think about anything, because Miller breaks every single popular trope, and I loved it! And secondly, she does it in such a great way, leaving small hints and pieces of information that only leaves you wanting more. Any author who wants to know how to hook a reader should take lessons from Linsey Miller, because she has it down to an art. The plot had me hooked from the first page! As I mentioned earlier, the plot started out a bit slow, but not slow enough that it was ever boring. Instead, that slow start worked as build-up, and the tension and action only intensified from that point. It grew and grew and grew, until I had trouble breathing and reading at the same time. The writing is bursting with tension. The writing is seriously amazing. No matter what type of scene it is, there was always a ton of tension in the writing, and I swear my heart never stopped beating frantically in my chest. The writing just had that unique quality that is hard to put your finger on that has the reader on the edge of their seat, holding their breath, anxious for what's going to happen next. I can go on and on about everything that was amazing about this book, but the truth is, no matter how great the plot, characters or romance is, in order to enjoy a book to this extent, that tension in the writing has to be there, or you won't enjoy it that much. And Miller's writing has it and so much more! This is a book everyone should read! It's filled to the brim with emotion, and it is honestly incredible how well Miller portrays every feeling, making it hard to separate the characters' feelings from your own. With relatable characters, world-building that is out-of-this-world, and tension from the first page, Mask of Shadows will take you on a journey that you won't forget. But a piece of advice before you start reading (and you need to read it, okay? Just do it); make sure to read it on a day you have free, because you will not be able to put it down.

Before starting this book, I had vague memories of the plot from a Wishbone episode many years ago. I was amazed at how good of a science fiction story this is, especially as it was written over 100 years ago. The Time Machine tells the story of a Victorian-era man who claims to be a time traveler. Having gathered his friends, he begins his story, which makes up the majority of the novella. The Time Traveler creates a time machine that travels hundreds of thousands of years into the future, where he discovers that humanity as he knew it, has changed dramatically, with humans evolving over time into the Eloi and the Morlocks. The story serves as a social commentary on the division between the upper class and the working class, as the time traveler theorizes that the two races descended from these groups of people. I wasn't a huge fan of the Time Traveler character -- he seems to jump to the conclusion that the Eloi are innocent and the Morlocks evil without much consideration, definitely seems to think himself superior to both these races, doesn't seem all that bothered about setting a huge forest fire that takes several lives, and somehow avoids death multiple times, including when visiting a future where the sun no longer shines. At the time of the publication, he might have been a relate-able character to readers, but now he seems the stereotypical middle-aged, upper-middle class male, and while you know he's going to make it back to his own time to tell his story to his friends, part of me was hoping the Morlocks would get to him, because he was getting annoying. Despite the character of the Time Traveler, I did enjoy this book, and the social commentary made is still relevant today. It's a quick read -- I listened to the audio book during the work day -- and well worth it if you enjoy science fiction.

This review was first posted on http://rubysreads.com. I've told you about my Bookish Preference for twins, so I imagine you know (or can guess) that Beautiful Lies was an auto-read for me. The story goes like this: identical twins Rachel and Alice are " 'monochorionic, monoamniotic twins,' which means [they] are identical twins who grew in the same amniotic sac and shared one placenta" (p.18). It's a real thing. I Googled it. Yet, despite this rare closeness, in the recent months, Rachel and Alice have grown apart. Rachel has become the "good twin," while Alice has begun acting out in the usual ways-drinking, wearing heavy makeup, hanging out with lowlifes (one in particular) and getting arrested. Okay, maybe the latter isn't "usual." Then one of the twins goes missing, and nobody believes it when the other twin insists that her sister is in danger. I haven't read any of Jessica Warman's books before, so I approached this one with few expectations-just a pleasurable hum of anticipation. And I'm happy to report that it was a solid read. Except...the description gives a few of the twists and turns away. Personally, I think unreliable narrators work best when we're not told up front that he or she is unreliable. It's a tool that's effective when we are left to discover it for ourselves...not when we are told that it's going to happen. Then, the narrator isn't unreliable because I never relied on them in the first place. You know what I mean? It's hard for me to review this book without giving away some of the important elements, so I'm going to keep things as brief as I can. The writing here is good, but not inspired. I didn't particularly like the narrator, and I didn't really sympathize with her. I felt that she was selfish. SPOILER: Particularly in her decision to keep quiet about her sister when she first went missing. She knew that if she told her aunt and uncle who she really was, they would have called the police right away. So why did she keep quiet? I also would have preferred to hear the story from the other twin's perspective. And don't get me started on the ending. It was abrupt and too unresolved. Beautiful Lies doesn't make me want to go glom Jessica Warman's backlist, but I won't reject anything she wrote out of hand, either.

When Quinn Collins set out to live on her own, she answered an ad for a roommate and moved in with Esther Vaughan never dreaming that Esther would turn out to become her best friend. Then one morning she awakes to the sound of Esther's alarm going off but Esther's not in her room and her bedroom window is wide open to the freezing cold Chicago air. Surely she didn't climb down the fire escape in the middle of the night! Quinn waits in vain for Esther to return but it doesn't happen. It seems that Esther has disappeared! Was she kidnapped? Did she run away from something? Quinn idolizes Esther and she can't imagine what has happened to her. She enlists the help of her friend Ben from work and tries to figure out where Esther is. But the more Quinn tries to puzzle through what happened to Esther, the more she realizes how little she really knows about her friend. She's beginning to think that Esther is not the saint that she always imagined. Meanwhile, in a small town near Lake Michigan, a young man named Alex Gallo has given up his dream of college to take care of his father who became a good-for-nothing drunkard when his mother left. He spends his hopeless days working as a dishwasher in the Priddy's cafe. One day a new customer comes in and she's a young woman he has never seen around town before. Alex gives the woman the name "Pearl" and he finds her to be quite an intriguing mystery. He sets his sights on finding out more about her. But Alex's boredom and loneliness may be leading him down a dangerous road. Don't You Cry is full of suspense and the details of each storyline will keep the reader guessing right up until the end. Piece by piece the puzzle falls into place until the big reveal. This is one of those where you think you have it all figured out but you never quite get there. A fast-paced and compelling read! Really, I suppose they come back to life again in the hands of someone who really cares about them. Anyway, because he has never heard of Carax he wants to know what happened to him. In many ways, Daniel and Carax's lives reflect each other. It is really exciting how Carlos Ruiz Zafon weaves the different pieces of information, misinformation and action together. The only reason I rated it four stars was because there were times when something didn't quite fit the way I thought it could (always very slight and nothing anyone but nitpicky old me would notice)- and I predicted who the man with no face was from the introduction of him. Reviewed by: Barb Genre: M/M Contemporary 4 Hearts See Review Here: Hearts On Fire Reviews Facebook link: https://www.facebook.com/pages/Hearts... Review: This anthology features stories related to the medical profession. Of the fourteen stories included, I found five to be outstanding, and I'd rate each of those 4.5 or 5 hearts. "Doctor in the Desert" by S.C. Wynne - An excellent story of a doctor in a small town hospital ER who meets one of the new cops in town when there's a disruptive patient in the ER. They see each other a few times at work before Trace, the doc, asks Logan, the cop, out for a drink. The story was well-written, with a touch of humor. I appreciated the fact that the author managed to fit in a brief story, a date, sex, and a serious morning-after discussion, all within the bounds of the pages of a short story. There wasn't insta-love but they did make a commitment to work toward a relationship. "Iron Man" by Meg O'Brien - Another excellent story about Aidan, a young man who was blinded in an auto accident and Bryan, the son of his neighbor who happens to be a blind rehabilitation specialist. Bryan offers to work with Aidan at no charge because he's completely captivated by not only his looks, but his intelligence, and his personality, by the time their first meeting is complete. He knows if he charges a fee, then Aidan will be a client, and he won't be able to date him. I like the way the author allowed a great deal of time to go by before there was any romantic involvement. And she definitely gave them the promise of a HEA and some nice non-erotic love scenes to spice up the story. "Hero Worship" by Kris T. Bethke - Alex, a paramedic, literally saves the life of the groom's younger brother, Matt, at his best friend, Carrie's, wedding. Matt has always had a case of hero worship for Alex and that just gets worse now, causing Alex to shy away because he's older and that's not a good foundation for a relationship. When Matt offers to move in with him to make up for the rent money lost with Carrie leaving, Alex initially hesitates, then reluctantly agrees. The story takes place over several months as the author allows the two to grow into more than friendship. Eventually, after several interesting twists in the story, the two get their HEA. "Tourniquet" by Kaye P. Hallows - A doctor is injured in the Boston Marathon bombing when, after stopping to apply a tourniquet a young boy's leg, he's caught in a second explosion. There's quite a bit of flirtatious play between Em and his nurse, Kane, who ultimately confesses that he's been interested in getting closer to Em for six years. Fortunately, both uphold ethical behavior while Em is hospitalized, but when he's released, the two begin their plans to build a relationship on their foundation of friendship. "To the Next Level" by Laura Mathews - Cam is a retired Marine who lost his leg in his last deployment and is being trained in the use of his new prosthesis. His therapist is Travis, and as the two flirt and get to know one another, Cam starts to hope that he might be able to create a future with this man. It isn't until Cam is released from rehab, however, that the two finally are able to get together and the story ends with the promise of a possible HEA. The other stories in the anthology, in no particular order are: "Right-Hand Man" by Rob Rosen - A young man with a broken arm and his neighbor who happens to be an unemployed live-in nurse find sex, love and a long term commitment. 3 hearts "Mend What Is Broken" by Fil Preis - When a doctor falls asleep at the wheel of his car, an old love who was recently hired as an orthopedic surgeon takes over his care and they ultimately decide to pursue a relationship once the doctor is no longer a patient. 4 hearts "First and Last" by Sara York - Reunited after ten years, a young man takes the opportunity to apologize for his verbal gay-bashing teenage behaviors when his former classmate and crush returns to town as a doctor. They initiate a conversation which leads to dating and eventually to their HEA. 4 hearts "Differential Diagnosis" by Anna Martin -The producers of a popular TV series have decided to add a gay romance this year. When the men playing the parts are attracted in real life, the two keep their romantic interest private so that it doesn't affect their TV roles. Of course it gets out, but the two stay together in a long term commitment and likely will have their HEA. 4 hearts "In My Own Skin" - by Thea Nishimori A surprise blind date for a movie marathon weekend makes Chris uncomfortable because he can never get close to a lover. He eventually confesses to his date that he has psoriasis and goes into a very detailed description of what that skin condition looks like, down to the weeping sores on the genital area. I didn't find the story as much of a romance as it was a lesson on psoriasis, however the author did assure that the MCs would see each other again and may have a HEA. 2.5 hearts "Rx for Sex" by Bru Baker-- Two psychiatrists struggle to stay together long term when schedules conflict, and they never seem to find time together. One decides to prescribe sex as their cure, and they make the commitment to find time to be together every day, no matter what happens. 3 hearts "Kind" by Samuel Scott Preston - Rod is in training as a grad student athletic trainer but he's had to go back into the closet to do so, since he fears exposure would ruin his career. While taking care of Damon, an injured athlete, the two find so much in common they become very close. After a misunderstanding over Thanksgiving, I got lost in some of the reasoning behind the balance of the story. It didn't quite make sense to me, and the quick turnaround in behavior when the two meet again threw me off so I ranked this story lower for that reason. 2.5 hearts "Pain Management" by Brigham Vaughn - This story is about a massage therapist who is treating a man who suffers from terrible migranes. The massage helps but the man needs to have ongoing treatment so they can't date due to ethical considerations even though they seem to have insta-love. After undergoing an amazing new medical procedure, the patient is released so the two MCs are able to finally be together and find their HEA. 3 hearts "Night Shift" by Casey O'Neill - Det. Wayne Fisher is a cop who's been separated a year from his husband, Mike, a doctor, because Mike couldn't live with all of the near death experiences a cop can have. Of course, one more happens when Wayne is shot in a convenience store robbery but it helps Mike to see that he'd rather have Wayne with him than never knowing where he is. This was a nice story but fairly predictable in its outcome. 3.5 hearts Overall, the anthology was good and I'd recommend it to any lovers of M/M romance, especially those who like stories with medical personnel. This would also be a great book to take on vacation.

*eARC kindly provided by Harlequin Teen via NetGalley* *Full review can be found at Part of that World. There is just something about this world of faeries, talking cats, and fickle creatures that Julie Kagawa created that I just don't want to leave. But I was hesitant to start this series, because it's a spin-off. And I loved the other characters so much I wasn't sure if I'd like the new ones. Rating: 4 Stars! As soon as I finished The Lost Prince, I had to start this one. There is just something about her stories that draws me in from the beginning, and pulls me along until I'm staring at the end and wondering what the hell just happened. In this spin-off series, the focus is on Ethan, Meghan's half-brother who is all grown up now. In the first book, he's pulled back into the world of the Nevernever, and that time, he wasn't alone. He learned truths and spent much of the time brooding about how he hated Faery and how pissed he was at Meghan for leaving them. He's still a brooding, sarcastic guy in this book, but his attitude is more bearable. I still dislike how he makes himself the martyr and decides what's best for everyone. But he has nothing on Keirran. I thought for sure Kagawa was setting up a relationship between Ethan and Keirran that resembles what Ash and Puck have. But clearly, I've been wrong. It's never going to be like that, though Ethan reminded me of Ash; sarcastic, brooding, pushing everyone away. And Keirran reminded me of Puck; a trickster who likes trouble. It made me wonder, not in a good way, whether the author could write characters with only three types of personalities (Meghan and MacKenzie are very similar too, though I like Kenzie much better). But the characters are very complex, and in this one, Keirran became more like Ash. However, I have zero sympathy with the icy and cold Iron Prince. He did whatever he could for the love of his life, Annwyl, but I find that excuse doesn't fly with me anymore. I still can't BELIEVE how many people have been affected by Keirran's incredibly stupid, selfish, and destructive choices. In Lost Prince, I can't say I became as invested in these new characters as I was with Ash, Puck, and Meghan. They're starting to grow on me, but I still find myself wanting more interactions with the others, especially Ash and Puck. And now, with what happened in Iron Traitor, I'm unsure how to feel about them. Mostly, one in particular. Keirran. Ugh, that traitor. How could he? The plot follows a dangerous story-line where everything these characters do seem to make things worse. Keirran is determined to do whatever it takes to save Annwyl, even at the cost of starting a war and killing himself. Ethan is there to be the "reasonable" voice, although he needed to remind himself when enough was enough. Kenzie was her usual kickass self, and I love that their relationship just keeps developing into something concrete. I loved the cameos with Grim, Puck, and Ash. But ugh, I have no clue where this story-line is going, and it scares me! I love Julie Kagawa's writing and this world she's created. I seriously can't wait to read the third book!

Though I've never seen an episode of The Office or The Mindy Project, I still think Mindy Kaling is pretty top notch. Whether intentionally or unintentionally, she's managed to successfully break the mold on the Hollywood clone machine. No longer must you be this tall, this thin, this white, etc. to ride the roller coaster that is being a success on primetime television. So why the two-star rating? Because Mindy's book bored me to tears. Her life, sadly, just didn't interest me all that much. Her meteoric rise to stardom seemed to have very few (very minor) hurdles. This is great for Mindy, I'm sure, but it doesn't exactly make for a scintillating story. I will admit that every now and then I'd find myself chuckling at one of her spot on observations about life or people but these little gems are sprinkled mildly throughout the book. The rest are dull essays about her life (past and present) and random lists. Yes, lists. Things like alternative titles for the book, expectations for a best friend, re-caps of comedic moments in television and film, and descriptions of pictures in her Blackberry. Listen, Mindy, I really don't care what you call your book. You and I are never going to be best friends so this particular insight into your personal code of friend ethics is totally pointless and not all that funny. I've seen Anchorman. I know it is hilarious when Ron Burgandy gets stuck in that glass case of emotion. I watch SNL. I'm very familiar with Chris Farley's much missed brand of physical comedy. I enjoy his Matt Foley skits as much as the next guy. I don't need you to re-cap them for me, I have YouTube for that. And even if I hadn't seen these great moments in comedy, I don't think you trying to explain them briefly in a list would do them any justice. As for the pictures in your phone... no one wants to see that. Seriously, when is the last time you got amped up about a friend whipping their phone out to show you pictures of anything? Half the time, I'm not even interested in the pictures in my own phone. I look through the massive folder of images and ask myself why I took a picture of a public toilet or if it is really necessary to have that many photos of my dog. All in all, it just wasn't for me. No cohesive format. Mediocre essays. A whole lot of useless filler. I expected much better and I was really disappointed.
So dire it doesn't really deserve a rating.

3.5 stars Ahhh, I'm a little bummed out at how this turned out. Picking up Messenger of Fear, something I have been anticipating since, oh, last year, I expected a more complex plot with mysterious characters and fabulous world-building. And although I got the mysterious aspect of it all, nothing else came close. Mara wakes up in this strange place, believing that she's dead. But she remembers nothing else other than her name. Then, she comes across the Messenger, who refuses to reveal to her exactly what is going on. Only that 1) He punishes the people who are guilty of something but aren't caught, and 2) there's something significant about the suicide of Samantha Early. So cool, we meet a bunch of cool characters. Mara, who's apparently the apprentice, the Messenger, who makes the guilty play a game of life and death, and then Oriax and Daniel, who I wish I knew who they were really. The reason why this novel didn't turn out as expected was because it only followed the flashback of Samantha and how she came to commit suicide. There wasn't anything about how the Messenger came to be, or who Oriax and Daniel were, and why and how they can do such things. I would forgive the book if it was a series, BUT NO, this is a standalone. I'm pretty sure. Though with that said, I did not see that twist at the end. I mean I should've, but I didn't. So as I said, I had no idea that the emphasis would be on bullying, which I never really like to read about because it pains me. But it did have a very good message, kind of. I mean in the way that bullying isn't something that should be tolerated because it can push someone to suicide. Which is sad. And it needs to stop. But when it comes to this book, I wasn't expecting so much on Samantha Early. I just wanted more on everyone else. This was a very fast read that although I enjoyed, didn't meet all my expectations. Honestly I was expecting something similar to A Darker Shade of Magic, but we can't all get what we want. This is a hard book to rate, because it's well written yet lacking in some aspects, but it's not necessarily bad either. I definitely suggest reading this and forming your own opinion.

Fantastic start to a new series! The idea of using matchmaking to control the world around you is an intriguing one. Of course, the practice of entering into a marriage for political alliance and gain is something that's been around since practically the dawn of time, but this book takes it one step further. Imagine an entire empire that is required by law to submit to matchmaking, and any "self-matched" couples are shunned and treated like lepers. Our heroine, Sage, is the offspring of self-matched parents, which resulted in her mother's parents disowning their daughter. Sage and her parents live a pleasant life, even though everyone around them looks upon them with disdain. When her parents die, Sage is forced to go live with her uncle, who tries--and fails--to make her conform to the society's notion of a marriageable miss. I mean, could you imagine the horror of a female who is interested in the sciences instead of how best to tilt her head in order to catch a husband. *rolls eyes* When Sage is recruited to be the high matchmaker's apprentice she dives into her job with gusto. She never imagined that her powers of observation would capture the royal army's notice, leading them to enlist her help as their spy. Here the story takes so many twists and turns that I don't want to spoil. Suffice to say, it was a white-knuckling experience. I loved all the secret identities and code names, although I did suspect that "Mouse" wasn't exactly who he claimed to be. The only thing that bummed me out and made me yell at the book (true story!) was Charlie (If you've read the book you know what I'm talking about). Recommend to all fantasy lovers.

Another good installment So as to not make us become too tired of Raphael and Cyn, D.B. Reynolds shifts focus from the west coast to the east coast, taking us from Malibu, California to New York City. While Raphael makes his business rounds, meeting with the master of New York City, Rajmund Gregor, he brings Cyn along to meet her good friend, Professor Sarah Stratton, who came down from upstate New York to visit. All is well until Rajmund and Sarah bump into each other at their party, and their lives won't ever be the same. While Raj is the master of The Big Apple, the official Vampire Lord Krystof rules the entire northeast territory from Buffalo. Succumbing to the mandess that comes with age, Krystof has made his territory vulnerable, motivating Raj to consider challenging him for power. He has to bear this pressure as well as solve a mystery involving the disappearances of a string of women. Police believe vampires are involved, so to exonerate his people it's up to him to solve it. Sarah Stratton has her own little secret as well; she has a strange psychic connection to these women. So to help save them she teams up with Raj, but both of them are in over their heads, ending up with more than they bargained for, including each other. This book is actually very good. I wasn't sure if I'd be interested in another couple other than Raphael and Cyn, but it really worked out quite well and Reynolds timed the change of scenery perfectly. I liked Rajmund's character. He's got a younger air about him than Raphael and he's working his way up towards becoming a Lord, so that was a little more refreshing. While Raphael is the most powerful of the North American Vampire Lords, he's not the only one, so it's good to explore other territories since some are evil like Jabril and Krystof, and it's interesting to see if and how these characters meet their overtimely demise. Sarah isn't as physically capable as Cynthia since she's only a professor, but she's smart and has a checkered past of her own. There's a lot of chemistry between these two from the beginning, but of course we never get a pay off right away with these books, and the series is better off for it. Again, I'm not the biggest PNR fan so I prefer that we don't get it out of the gate. As always with this series, the cover doesn't live up to the quality of the story. Sure, there's beefcake, but again the design is amateurish and I really have to wonder who illustrates them. This is probably the worst one so far. I can barely even read the subtitle written across his head. The storyline is okay, but after a while once you've read these books back to back like I have, it becomes a bit of a pattern so I found my attention wandering here and there, but it wasn't too significant. Though it isn't too bad, I think I'd like to see this series branch out from mysteries about missing women, which was also the mystery for its predecessors. I would like to see more fighting because the action is well done and it keeps the adrenaline going. All in all, these are easy and entertaining reads and the quality has remained consistent through book 3, so I'll continue to recommend this series at this point. *Review also posted to Amazon.

This is the second book in a row that I've read that I've been someone torn on. You see, like What Happens Next, the good elements of this book were phenomenal. I'll go into more details later, but Sloane's mental state and the raw character interactions were some of the best I've ever read. This almost made it to my list of all-time favorites. But there were also elements that bothered me, enough that I couldn't put it on the list. Granted, the bad elements here were fewer and further between than the ones in What Happens Next. But they were still present, and the book would've been better without them. But right off the bat, the book is excellent. The book is told from Sloane's point of view, and ever since her sister ran away and left her with her abusive father, she's been suicidal. Summers's portrayal of Sloane's mental state is very accurate and poignant. In everything Sloane does, everything she thinks about, Lily and her father and her suicide are in the back of her mind. Her attitudes to it are appropriately bitter, but unlike some books about suicide I could name, Sloane is still very sympathetic. All of this comes through most noticeably in the prose. It's written in present tense, giving us the impression that we're seeing Sloane's thoughts and actions as she has them. On a very consistent basis, her thoughts are completely believable and interesting. It helps that the prose goes into stream-of-consciousness in some of the more emotional moments. It was here that I was most strongly affected, most constantly aware of how well-rendered Sloane is, where I was the most moved. Because of all this, reading This is Not a Test is a truly unique and immersive experience. Nowhere else have I ever seen anything like this, but I'd love to. Which is why I'm going to be reading another Summers book at some point. Another thing the prose did that I loved so much, that made the reading experience so unique, is that it purposely kept little things from us, so that we were constantly surprised. This rarely kept me at an arm's length from the story, because the things that Summers kept from us were never necessary to the story, and we were given enough information to enjoy the individual scenes. Instead, this technique left me guessing, and enjoying the book further. I suspect that this technique won't appeal to everyone, but it certainly did to me. There were a few prose problems - Summers occasionally used sentence fragments or run-ons, making the prose choppy at some points and runny in others - but the other prose elements far more than made up for it. Most of the other characters were as well-rendered and interesting as Sloane. The one exception was Harrison; I kept waiting for Summers to add more depth to his character, to develop him beyond a crybaby stereotype, and it just never happened. But everyone else is great. In particular, I really loved Trace's character arc; his parents were killed on the journey he and the others took to the school, and he blames Cary for their loss. Trace isn't always entirely sympathetic, but his mental state is always fascinating. Likewise, Cary, Rhys, and Grace are also interesting in their reactions to the apocalypse and their desire for, above all else, survival. It reminded me of The Way We Fall, only more intense; Crewe redeemed her characters and their mental states, but Summers is merciless to them. (Not that this makes The Way We Fall any less effective - the books are both honest portrayals of two completely different situations.) Summers's eye for characters and their psychology is almost flawless. Because of all this, the plot isn't very action packed, and it doesn't have a traditional dramatic structure. The dramatic structure is built entirely around the characters' emotions. I'm sure some readers who are less interested in psychology and emotions will find the plot boring; after all, they don't have to work too hard to survive, and the events that happen often occur simply to give the characters an interesting situation. It's most notable in the enemy - this is technically a zombie novel, but we don't actually see that many zombies, until the very end. Yet there's still an overarching sense of tension. The characters are still aware of the constant threat around them; after all, that's what they're reacting to. Summers created a tense situation and characters to respond to it; I need nothing more from my books. But remember when I said that there were a few problems that prevented me from considering this one of my favorites? Because there were a couple, even apart from the minor ones that I mentioned above. I said before that the story rarely kept me at an arm's length, but occasionally it did. The biggest way was probably in the worldbuilding; we never get a clear picture of the exact effects the virus that created the zombies, and I never quite understood their exact capabilities. We see so little of the world around Sloane and her friends, it's hard to say whether it made sense or not. However, that problem is insignificant compared to the biggest problem: there's no theme. There's lots of potential for a theme (the heroine is suicidal, for the love of god), but Summers never really says anything about her situation, other than "This is what it's like to be suicidal." The same goes for the rest of the character interactions: Cary's sex with Lily and involvement with drugs, Tracy's slow decline... all of it should lead up to some grand message, but it never does. I wouldn't want the message to be anvilicious, John Green style, but I want something, and I never got it. That causes a lack of focus in the character interactions; without something for Summers to say, there's nothing her to focus on. And if that's the case, what's the point? Why read about characters in such a depressing situation if it's not going to teach me something about life? Still, that doesn't change the fact that the book is beautifully written, with wonderful character interactions. Reviewers more familiar with the zombie-apocalypse genre than I have said that this book didn't add much new to the genre for them, and that they'd recommend it for people who aren't familiar with the genre. Well, this is my first zombie book, and I loved it. So if you're like me in that regard, this is definitely the book for you. You'll love it, I promise.

All the Light We Cannot See is a novel I probably wouldn't have bought when out looking for something new to read, but it was an Indiespensable pick sent to me by Powells book store. Despite all of the hype it was getting at the time, it's been sitting on my shelves for a long time now unread. However, earlier in the year, a number of people in my book group thought they'd might like to read it, so I took it out, cleaned off the shelf dust and read it, since it's the first book-group read after our summer hiatus. In the meantime, the book won the Pulitzer, so I was, of course, pretty eager to get to it. Once again, I a) am torn in my reaction towards this novel, and b) find that I am once again the proverbial fish swimming upstream against the tide of readers who LOVED this book or thought it was the best novel they'd read all year. There are spoilers below, so proceed at your own risk. Let's get the positives out first. I think Mr. Doerr is a good writer, although there are a lot of issues around structure and plot points that I have with this book. There were moments where I couldn't help but to get caught up in the story because, well, I love reading about this period in history. Describing the panic, the uncertainty, and the realization of the French people that the Nazis were in their country to stay was very well done, and I especially enjoyed the sections describing the steps taken to safeguard national treasures in the museum of natural history. I felt Doerr was at his very best though when writing the scenes depicting Werner's time in the Hitler Youth academy -- when these scenes cut to another, I couldn't wait to get back to them. My god. I was just floored at how young children were taken into this place -- where "only the purest, only the strongest" would be admitted -- and then taught most brutally that weakness of any sort would not be tolerated. And then, there's the story of Frederick, who refuses to become like everyone else; what happened to him just about had me in tears. To me, if the author had written only about the Hitler Youth academy and the things that happened there combined with Frederick's story, that would have made for beyond-excellent, gut-wrenching reading. On the other hand, I wasn't too far into the novel before I realized that overall, this is a YA story set in Occupied France. I'm not very fond of YA novels as a general rule, and as the whole book is playing out I'm seeing the movie running through my head with the brightest young stars of today (I don't know who they are since I don't really watch this sort of thing) playing the lead roles of Werner and Marie-Laure. Second, and in one of the most unforgivable aspects of this novel, I knew exactly how this story was going to play out, after Marie-Laure's great-uncle Etienne revealed himself as the voice behind the radio broadcasts Werner and Jutta used to listen to as children. Considering that that happens on page 159, there really isn't much left in the way of surprises in this book. Third, I don't get the way the author cut his story timewise. Normally time shifts don't bother me, but this time around I found myself having to go backwards in the novel to remember what happened in what year. It's jagged and extremely disconcerting, but even worse, it makes absolutely NO SENSE. Yes, yes, I know, it's one of everyone's favorite books, but it definitely wasn't one of mine. I also figure I'll be the only one not going gaga over it at this month's book group meeting, opening myself up to whatever scorn the rest of the women want to heap upon me. Sorry - I just can't help it.

Intangible begins with a prediction, one that Luke has to see no matter how much he fears the result. He faces an eerily beautiful woman, and a raveling mystery of his birth -- "Shall she be the first to die, Seer?" In a world of vampires, elves, ghosts, and gifted humans, Sera and Luke find themselves in grave danger for they may very well be the downfall of the Realm. Soon, creatures of the Realm close in on Luke and Sera. When Sera unwittingly heals a vampire into human... There goes peace and stability! Sera comes face to face with vampires, mind-readers and ghosts who are determined to remove her from their sight once and for all. The brother and sister must find out what the prophecy bestows upon them before Luke loses his chance to save his sister's future. Before it's too late. Was it their gift? Or their curse? Using varying perspectives, J. Meyers allows us a little insight to every character. Not too much, just enough to keep you curious and suspended and asking for more! We have the protective and helpful Fey, sly and mysterious Marc, creepy yet softhearted Jonas, and not forgetting our lovely pair of twins: Luke and Sera! If anything, they are the cutest siblings I've ever seen, full of understanding, trust and love for each other. I enjoyed their witty banters and poking fun that eased up many tense/awkward moments. They tend to always know when the other is troubled, so they stick through thick and thin no matter what. The strong chemistry between them is something difficult to find and even more so when we're talking about family and not love interests! Ahhh... Love interests. We don't get much romance here, but point is, that's no longer the key of the story! With a looming prophecy as background, Sera gets her little taste of romance, only that her feelings are misplaced on the one whose intention is to betray her to the Shadows, Marc. Brief moments when Jonas feels a sense of familiarity around Sera got me giggling at his jealousy, I'm foreseeing a love triangle in the sequels! Luke, on the other hand, doesn't get much luck at love, but I think I see sparks fly somewhere... ;) Though there are times when the plot turns predictable, many other surprises await you with unexpected twists! J. 's writing is natural and smooth, bringing you along with her words in no time at all, just add a faster-paced build up to the climax and this book will be well on its way to the Map of Wonder!

Here's the thing. This is apparently another "author behaving badly" and everyone thinks that he should die a fiery death. If anything this seems more like a case of an author using a negative review in a way to send a positive message to other writers. In no part of his post does he personally attack or name drop and where other people are seeing condescension I'm seeing a statement of fact so I'm still willing to give him a chance. If anything, the fact that his book is allegedly so markedly different than most other YA literature makes me actually want to read it. If I hate it, I hate it but if it works for me, cool. Here's a link to the thread so you can read the article and decide for yourself: http://classof2k13.com/2013/05/08/clo... And here's the author's response to all of this: "Hi, all. Let me first repeat from above: "My sale doesn't discount this reader's reaction. "Good" or "bad" is always up to each individual, and I've collected (and expect to collect) strong votes on both sides with this book." -- And there is nothing in my post that was meant to suggest otherwise. Readers can (and will) dislike my books. Not once above do I suggest the reviewer was "wrong" or "misread" or...etc. Not once do I suggest the reader is ANYTHING other than someone who gave the book a shot and decided "No Thanks." This blog was -- in a post specifically for writers and future writers -- meant only to say: yes, some readers are probably going to dislike your book, but as long as you write the book you want to, some readers are probably going to like it also. That's not "dismissive" of the reader who didn't like your book. It's the exact opposite. It's stating that 'good' or 'bad' is up to EACH reader and there WILL be folk on both sides. I meant nothing else. In class all the time, I'll ask the students if they liked our last book or not. And half don't and half do... and then we discuss why on both sides and say "OK, what's the next book?" Done. I expect no different for my books. Maybe that's why I clearly felt too comfortable talking about a negative review. It never occurred to me that doing so was somehow an attack on the reviewer. All day long, I dialogue about books with readers. What sucks here, of course, is the internet. In person, the reviewer could say to me, "I hated X, Y and Z" and I'd groan and say "Shoot! I totally put in X, Y and Z on purpose" and hopefully one or both of us would laugh and then discuss some other book. The end. Alas... As to why THIS review: I thought the line about the clone party was funny (in a good way) and couldn't get that image out of my head and so used it to frame a blog. That's all. It was not an "attack" but a public recognition of the fact that my book's "difference" is clearly gonna fail for some readers. These readers are NOT wrong. They are NOT people who "just don't get it." They're just readers who didn't like a book. And that's ok. Saying so is not meant to be offensive or attacking at all... and I'm sorry if anyone thought otherwise. Ok, all. Good night. Let me clearly say again before vanishing: Readers are welcome to dislike books and call out things they hate. Their opinion is just as valuable as those who like the book. And I believe this so much... I thought I could reference such a review as easily as if I were referencing a glowing one. Hopefully, a better explanation of my intentions above..."

First, feel free to disregard my review -- I'm not in nor have I ever been in the target audience (13 year old girls). Message: Good Fantasy/Sci-Fi have a great didactic message. I cannot find a single positive message in the story. The primary lesson I can find is that you are a slave to forces greater than yourself and you should just perform your role or go live in isolation. We spend most of the novel building Katniss' understanding that she can be a leader, yet in the end she is nothing but a pawn who acts but never leads. After the war she retreats from any responsibility and accepts what is handed her while living in fear for her children. Great message.... Surprise Ending: The target of Katniss' last arrow of the war is so obvious that it was painful. Love Triangle: painful and boring -- and again Katniss doesn't make a choice she just accepts what happens World: What is the point of District 12? Supposedly they produce coal to power the other Districts and Capital -- but no one seems to care that there is no more coal. If the coal isn't necessary to power the nation than why was anyone mining coal? War: What is the point of conquering District 2 and the Capital -- they produce nothing necessary and thus should quickly starve, run out of power, and materials (except stone). Why bother fighting street to street through high tech (and bizarre) traps in the Capital when they just need to lay siege? Combat: Machine guns can't do anything against the hover-bombers, but explosive arrows wreak havoc? WTF? Bizarre Hunger Games' traps are not a good way to defend your city. Katniss: The never ending self-evolvement is REALLY boring. Makeup and Clothing: If I read more about makeup and fashion, I may give up reading altogether. There a few points when Katniss is brought out and she acts, but there are very few and the reader needs to slog through pages of whining, irrelevant blather, and idiocy. Sigh....

*I received this book from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review* I really wanted to like this book. I loved J.A. I did really enjoy how Elias and Bray loved each other. I think that was amazing, and I loved that they were willing to do whatever they could for each other. Bray was just so messed up, and it bothered me that she was willing to take Elias down with her. For me being in love with someone is being selfless, but the whole book Bray was overly selfish. I also started feeling like there were alot of similarities with some other New Adult books I had read. Especially Bray's bipolar disorder, I just really felt like there was another character that she seemed modeled after. It also bothered me at the end how Bray went from horribly suicidal to suddenly being fine. Granted it was the epilogue, but I didn't get to see her transition from one to the other and so it felt disjointed. Overall, I did really enjoy this book, and I love Redmerski's writing style. I was sucked in the whole way, but the character of Bray just fell flat for me. I give Song of the Fireflies 3 out of 5 stars, because it did draw me in, even if I didn't love everything. *This review was first posted to Moonlight Gleam Reviews http://moonlightgleam.com/2014/02/son...*

Perhaps one of the most jarring, exquisite, books I've read all year. I don't where to start but I can say this: The alternating povs of the past and present were amazing. Not only did it navigate the reason for the main plot; it navigated through all the characters. Every single one fleshed out completely. The phrase "morally grey" does not begin to explain the mold of these characters. Each one of them, terribly, terribly flawed- maybe to the exception of Sydney- but, nonetheless, no one in this book has that hero flare, the kind you really root for. And it's funny, considering it is a book about superheroes. But superheroes is the lightest term that could possibly be thought of. Especially when it's titled Vicious . The book follows the darkness, the gritty, raw parts of you that you don't want to touch. The type of parts that is concealed. The kind of aching that devoid you of emotion. No character is left untouched; the darkness is everyone and it's unleashed one way or another. I loved loved how Schwab captured that concept. The characters were written tragically, painfully. hollow and broken. There was no room for the lightness that superheroes (or the concept of) usually bring because this book wasn't about hope; it was about revenge and the satisfaction of a kill. It's scary reading this book, how empty and numb these characters can really get, but I think that's what made this book so good, Schwab never held back and I'm so glad for it.

*Update 06/12* My thoughts have changed about the book and my rating has been lowered. I am unable to explain why though, due to reasons which are not allowed to be stated because they are in conflict of GR policy of what is/is not allowed in a review. *Original Review for the book 10/11* Flat-Out Love definitely falls more on the "girly" side, but I enjoyed it almost as much as I enjoyed Anna and the French Kiss. The story follows a girl named Julie who is swindled out of her money when she gets to Boston and finds out that the college apartment she had reserved does not exist. An old friend of her mom's living nearby steps in and invites her to live with them - in the home of a completely dysfunctional family that is falling apart. Julie manages to take refuge in the emails and Facebook updates (some of which are completely funny) of the brother whose room she is staying in while he's off "traveling the globe." I don't blame her for falling for Finn, the human version of a cardboard cutout named "Flat Finn" that the little sister drags around because she's missing her brother. Then you have the complete math geek brother who can be a pain most of the time, but you can tell he's hurting inside as well because he shoulders a lot of responsibility for the family, which also makes you want to know more about him. I can not begin to explain this book well enough to do it justice. There was so much more to the story than I was expecting when I started. It always makes a book more special for me when an author can take the reader through a range of emotions, making you giddy and smiling one moment, and feeling the sting of hurt the next. Just by the name and summary, I figured that Flat-Out Love was going to be a light and potentially funny read, and it was. But there was a lot of heartache bubbling under the surface, which I hadn't planned on. If you're one of those people who feels like you've been reading the same story over and over, then you'll want to pick up this book. It's definitely different from anything else I'd recently read.

For me, the impact of this book is observing how alike the protagonist (Christopher, a 15 year old who is diagnosed as having Asperger's syndrome) and the rest of us 'normal people' are. I use the term 'normal' as being able (to some extent) to relate to others. On the surface, we are not alike with Christopher (as 'we' don't regularly meltdown around others). But this book (by using Christopher as the first person writer of this book) delves us deeply into Christopher's world. The author uses his experience (in working with children like Christopher) to do this. I presume that the author's main purpose of writing this book is to truthfully 'bridge the gap' between 'Asperger's syndrome people' and 'normal people', and perhaps the author is trying to spark us to be more empathetic overall. We are alike with Christopher in that we have dreams, goals, hang-ups, and surrounding dysfunction. But we can 'disguise' our hang-ups enough (or our hang-ups aren't so 'profound') in order to function around other people without much trauma (whereas Christopher is prone to meltdown and cause a 'scene' when he 'goes off script' or deals too intimately with others). Christopher finds comfort in working math problems, whereas we might comfort in reading 'People magazine' 'watching TV', etc. Man, I would have been so good at math if I wasn't so uncomfortable at working hard math problems! I think the book is very effective in relating me to Christopher, as I was very happy when accomplishes his goals. Unfortunately, Christopher's parents are not so aware of what Christopher is thinking and they have their own 'agendas', so they don't share in Christopher's joys. And Christopher really can't relate his joy to others anyways. The book's strength (of using Christopher's point of view) is also a weakness (at least it is for me). Even though the book is short, Christopher's 'claustrophobic' and 'selfish' world view (Me, Me, Me, Me) wears me down after a while. It would have been daring (and pehaps too ambitious to pull off) to write a book like this with multiple points of view. Other books have done this (Let The Great World Spin is the first book that comes to mind) and I have very much enjoyed the multiple perspectives. When I use the term 'point of view', I would even have liked to see Christopher's point of view at a later time in his life (as this book is constrained to a few weeks of Christopher's life). I am aware that individuals with Asperger's can learn to effectively interact with other people. I have heard second-hand (from someone I know) of a person with Asperger's who learned how to interact with others through watching the body language of movies. This person has become so effective that those around him no longer think of him as a 'weirdo', but as 'normal'. Surely, not all "Asperger's individuals" can learn this, but it would make for an interesting read. One last thing about the book: As the wise and understanding teacher, Siobhan is so much an inspirational character. I enjoyed reading about Siobhan's interactions with Christopher. Siobhan is like a 'guardian angel' type of person to me. And even though Christopher couldn't directly express it, Siobhan was a very meaningful and impactful person in Christopher's life.
