Jen gave me this lovely book for Christmas, and it was the perfect way to start off the reading year. You're likely to hear the 'timeless children's book' descriptor a lot, and with good reason. It's timeless in the sense that it's a non-specified date in the past (early 1900s? Later 1800s?) when women were not cellists and were not supposed to wear trousers, but when it also feels perfectly right for a delightful man like Charles to rescue a baby, take her home and raise her, without bothering either of them with stupid things like school. It's also timeless in that same way because it could be a Noel Streatfield if he got in a Nanny to help out. Mostly, though, it made me think of A Little Princess, with a very different sense of social justice: no romanticizing of the diamond mines into something out of The Arabian Nights; no meek and grateful poor children, and no patient suffering. Sophie is a wonderful character, the rooftoppers she meets are heartbreaking and yet so strong, and I fell head over heels with Charles. It's whimsical and funny, too, which I don't think of A Little Princess as being, and yet ... that rooftop feast, for hungry Matteo (and Sophie, though hers was a voluntary hunger! ), had the same emotional payoff as the one from the earlier book. My only concern was that a bit of me wanted the ending tied up with a series of weatherproof (and not from pigeon fat) bows. So. There is now an epilogue in which Sophie's mother produces her birth cert, thereby clearing Charles, his scholarly work can be done perfectly well in Paris, and they set up a proper home for all the children together - one so free and with such perfect access to the rooftops that even Matteo feels safe there. I will not countenance Charles going back to London alone.

I'm debating whether or not to put 4 or 5 stars for this book...but then I think of the fact that I barely put it down since I started it and I really wish it wasn't over already and I realize it must be 5. It's a 5 star for me. Simply put, I found this book refreshing. At first I thought I was going to hate it. I thought that the writing was strange and Juliette thoughts were jumbled and I didn't think I would be able to make it through the whole thing. But then Adam came and things happened and suddenly I could not put the book down for the life of me. It's different, that's for sure; but different it a good--very, very good--way. Juliette is very real to me. Her most basic characteristic that draws you to her is the goodness of her heart. She is a good person. Even though she's been hurt, she doesn't want to hurt others. However, even she struggles with the attraction of power and how good it feels to have power. That conflict is realistic to me and it makes sense. Overall I found Juliette to be a fantastic heroine. I found myself quite agreeable to the way her mind works and her actions. In fact, all the characters are quite lovely. Even the complexity of Warren drew me in. I can't wait to see where all these characters take us. The first half or so of the story was a little slow, but it still kept me reading. There are drastic changes that occur at various points in the book, yet they are in their rightful place. It all works. I do find it a little typical that Adam and Juliette have basically been in love since they were children--quite like the Hunger Games, no? However, I'm not too concerned with that. Like everything else, it works. It wasn't cliched at all; actually, I thought the anticipation of the "cliche-ness" was addressed quite well. In all I liked this quite a lot. It was refreshing, different, and I'm rather in love with it all. Great way to start off reading during my Christmas Break.

Reviewing is serious business. Oh wait, it really isn't. You throw out a few words about your thoughts on a book and move on. Sometimes you like a book, sometimes you don't. Sometimes you don't even want to have to go into listing out all of the reasons in great detail (with quotes and pics to enthusiastically drive home the point) why you did or didn't like a book because you're just not all that passionate about your reasons in the first place. This is one of those times. Seduce was okay. Honestly. I don't have any big GRRRRRR feelings toward it. Yes, there was some extreme cheese phrasing. Yes, there were some typos. Yes, the guy sounded like a guy who was written by a female who was trying to sound like a guy (even extremely arrogant guys probably don't have that much internal dialogue about every single thing which makes them desirable - it kept coming back up just when I thought it was over). Yes, there were multiple scene breaks, to the point where I wondered if a smooth transition would ever be made. Yes, I felt like I'd read this story before in other books. But... none of those things made me think, "wow, this book sucks." Because the book honestly didn't suck. The story was extremely readable. This is where I blame my voracious reading appetite for my lack of enthusiasm. I read a lot. It's hard not to compare books, especially when similar plot twists in other books, have made me do the ugly cry. I didn't ugly cry here. Maybe it had something to do with the fact that I didn't feel any sort of all-consuming love happening, and those are the types of love stories which rip your heart out. We were told about the character feelings, we saw a lot of sex, then shit happened. Because we didn't have an entire book of watching two people falling in love, and didn't get to see much of their relationship outside of how compatible they were in the bedroom, I didn't have much to attach to. This was a shorter story about two people and their raging sexual attraction (and for the record, there's absolutely NOTHING wrong with that; in fact I like erotic short stories/novellas). I'm just noting that because I didn't have time to get to fall in love with the characters, this was why I didn't get hurt when the big "uh oh" happened. And since I gathered that this entire last part of the book was supposed to be what the hook was, I had a very "eh" reaction when it failed to hook me because I hadn't been emotionally invested. Call me spoiled by stories which have fired on all cylinders and have managed to get me emotionally invested in every single thing that was going on... because this story was nothing like that. However, Seduce was a sexy little quickie. Again, nothing wrong with that. I like sexy little quickies. And again, Seduce was completely readable. In fact, I am interested in reading the next book because I have the feeling that this story will impact huge character growth for the lead. With a little bit of editing/polishing, and a longer book (which I assume it will be, since this was a prequel short), I might find myself rooting for character happiness. *edit* Went to delete my notes and realized that I almost left out the obligatory "Stacia hates the overdone love/drug reference*... She was like a drug, an addiction.

I had heard so many things about The Iron Fey already that I simply had to start this series now, as it is the fairy month in my Paranormal Reading Challenge. Some people are gushing about this book all over the place, some seem to fiercely hate it. I guess, I'm somewhere in between. The Iron King is a very nice fairy story which kept me entertained but not engrossed. As usual, I'd like to start with what I really liked about it. In this case that would be the plot. This woman has some imagination, I was baffled. The plot is a non-stop action journey, Meghan's quest on her way to find her brother. The book is full of mysterious, fantastic creatures, wondrous worlds and fascinating characters. That alone is reason enough to be excited for the sequel. I really need to know how the story goes on. The cliffhanger is mean, as it is part of the concept, yet not unexpected. Now on to the characters. I've read in some reviews that Meghan is some whiny and annoying girl. I do understand why people would think so. But by way of exception, I don't agree, even though I'm quickly annoyed by whiny females. The sudden way Meghan's life changes and all the resulting events are enough to let the strongest woman despair. And there really is some character development in this book. Meghan finds her inner strength and her iron backbone. Then there is Ash who I truly adore. But I'm always into the vulnerable bad boys. His shell cracked more and more often and I loved that true Ash that was shining through those cracks. Nevertheless, I couldn't really get into the book. I know that sounds weird after I just said how full of suspense the plot was. But if there is just one exciting incident after the other, fight and argument and new evil creature and fight... it lacks a deeper sense. For me, it could have been less of those dramatic incidents and more focus on character relationships and other aspects. I also strongly disliked Puck. Can't see how anybody could find him funny or cute. In my eyes, he's just annoying. And I didn't feel ANY friendship vibe between Meghan and him. She constantly talks about him as his best friend. But to me, it seemed that her best friend vanished along with the name Robbie. Puck was a strangely distant character whose pranks were nothing but needless. I'm glad that I finally read this book. That enables me to be part of the discussions about it. I loooove discussing. So tell me what you thought of this book!

Lt. Grayson Masters wanted nothing more than to graduate on top of his class of the Apache Helicopter Course. Nothing can distract him from his goals, or so he thinks, until Samantha Fitzgerald became their new roommate, distracting him from everything possible. He doesn't need a hot, smart-mouth and free-spirited beauty who knows how to push his buttons. I love this guy despite the serious personality. He has his own secrets, most of them heartbreaking, and I wonder until when can he keep it? He separates his school life, his friends from his life back home, and there is a big reason why. Reasons I was not sure at first weather to applaud him or slap him. Nevertheless, he was trying to do what he thought was best. If our hot helicopter pilot has some secrets, our girl, Samantha Fitzgerald has some too. Fresh from being kicked out of the university, Samantha flew over a hundred miles to escape her past and start over. But how can she, when every time she opens a computer, it's staring her right in the face? Or every time knocks on the door, the past would stare back at her. But this girl is pretty much amazing, because she's holding herself together, her strength is pretty much admirable. There was no way her past is going to stop her, not if she can help it. And then there's the enigmatic Grayson, unlike the rest of the bunch, he's a bit cold and lacks charm, and she can't help but wonder why. They have chemistry, even during the first time that they met, and it was slowly burning. Although, their past wouldn't let them cross the thin line between friendship and being lovers. I was glad that they started out as friends at first. I gotta watch them falling helplessly in love one day at a time and fight off the intense attraction they have for each other. Grayson is not perfect, but you couldn't help but love him. He is strong, loyal and very much honorable. He does things one would not expect him to do, and despite the fact I would like to question it at times, I couldn't help but for my heart to just break right there. He was torn, and he wanted to do something about it, but he didn't want to hurt anyone that was important to him. I love the emotions that grip my heart throughout my read: it's a rollercoaster ride, exhilarating and addictive. Rebecca Yarros gives us another set of wonderful characters to pin and fall utterly in love with. Imperfect, but definitely people you can't help but love. It had me swooning, and I didn't have the heart to put down this book. With all the twist and turns, and what was happening between them, I couldn't miss anything!!! Every scene, every dialogues, every single word had me hooked. Like the rest of her series, this one was another great read. It's beautiful, beautiful read that can make and break your hearts. I highly recommend this one! "Grave Mercy" was a delightful change of pace for me. While the synopsis says that Ismae is 17, within a couple of chapters it jumps ahead a couple of years, so it was nice to have an older protagonist. After being treated poorly for the first 17 years of her life by men, Ismae is sure that all men are evil and is eager to do Mortain's bidding and dispatch them. Yet within moments of setting off with Duval it's all "oh, he's touching my waist *girly swoons*". Ok, slight exaggeration, but she is hyper aware of him being a guy and near her. Of course, it's not nearly as bad as a lot of YA novels are with the boy swooning, and I quite liked her growing relationship with Duval. You would just think that being a bad ass assassin and hating men would make her a little more wary of them. I did, however, love Ismae's extreme eagerness for wanting to kill people with walking into a room and hoping to find Mortain's marque (a mark on the body Mortain leaves to show her who to kill) on someone so that she can kill them. She's basically newly unleashed on the world and wants to prove herself to the convent. Robin LaFevers nicely builds on Ismae's character as she slowly starts to question who she's killing and why, and learns to understand the marque of Mortain. The book does get a little long at times, especially about 3/4 of the way through. There is a lot of politics and backstabbing as most of the story revolves around the Duchess Anne and all the men who want to marry her for her kingdom. Interestingly enough, I read in the Author's note that a lot of the characters and the circumstances of the book are based on actually events in history, which to me makes it all the more interesting. A good read, "Grave Mercy" is well written, and has some interesting characters, but does drag out a little in the middle. I received a free copy of this book in exchange for my honest review

Solid 5 Stars Let me start off by saying that I had absolutely no idea what to expect from this book. It was assigned for one of my college courses and the only thing I knew was that I had about a month to finish it and start in on my paper. By the time I finished this book, I was floored, heartbroken, and had fallen in love with it--certainly not something I expected to happen for an assigned reading. {Minor Spoilers! Beware!} Tell The Wolves I'm Home tells the the story of June, a young and awkwardly eccentric teen who has just suffered her greatest loss, losing her uncle to AIDS. June has a very close relationship with her Uncle, Finn, and as she has no other friends and her parents are mostly absent or dismissive of her through a majority of her life, it's understandable that the loss of Finn has left June with a gaping hole in her heart. However, Finn's boyfriend, Toby, suddenly begins contacting June and the two form a bond that may even rival the one June had with Finn. Together, through several bumps in the road, they overcome their grief and find comfort in each other's presence. I absolutely adored this book! I really loved June as she reminded me much of myself when I was her age, awkward and interested in niche things that not a lot of other people cared for or understood. Brunt's characterization of June was so realistic that it left me feeling almost raw. I also really enjoyed Toby. I'll admit I was a little weirded out by the fact that June's dead uncle's boyfriend started contacting her (a teenager) out of the blue, but the story managed to pull this together and explain it perfectly by the end. There are mention of taboo feelings in this book (ie. June's romantic love that she holds for her uncle and, then, Toby), but that is part of what made me love this book so much. These emotions are handled with expert care by Brunt and by the end of the novel, June has sorted through her feelings towards her uncle and Toby and has begun the mending process. Honestly, you just have to read it! It's emotional, heart wrenching, and powerful.

5 Stars: Hard to Hold on To by Laura Kaye is a novella in the Hard Ink series, fitting in right between books 2 and 3. It starts up in the moments following the end of book 2 and focuses on Easy and Jenna as they help each other cope with a bunch of emotional trauma. It's a wonderfully sweet story and my favorite of the series so far. This could be read as a standalone by those interested in the series and wary of committing to a full-length novel, but it has so much more to offer if you've read books 1 and 2 first! I cannot recommend this series enough if you are a fan of suspenseful contemporary romance! A quick note to series readers who are wondering if they can skip this one since it's a novella: Yes, technically, but why would you??? For one thing, while no major developments occur, plenty of minor ones do, and this story definitely progresses the series. For another thing, Easy and Jenna are AWESOME! Having just been rescued from a terrifying abduction, Jenna turns to Easy to help ground her during the panic she battles in the aftermath. They've had a connection since he was assigned as her protection detail for one night and the connection only grows as Easy helps her through the hardest few days of her life. Any man willing to handle the tears and vomit of a strange woman to whom he owed absolutely nothing was someone worth getting to know better. That had to be in a girls' guide to guys somewhere. Easy is still suffering from PTSD and depression after the ambush that resulted in the death of his best friend and his own discharge from the military. I loved the way Kaye approached depression in this story. She didn't shy away from the topic, one that is so prevalent among veterans, and she avoided the fairy tale ending of "true love immediately heals all wounds." While I have no doubt that Easy and Jenna will overcome the horror in their pasts, the story makes it clear that recovery is a long and difficult road that is best traveled with the help of others. She didn't heal what was broken within him--he wasn't that naive or delusional. But she sure as f**k made him remember the man he'd once been. Made him see glimpses of that man within the person he was right now. And made him believe maybe he could become that man again. On a lighter note, there are more tattoos! Easy has a variety of them, but the showstopper is the quote he gets along the right side of his rib cage: You were never created to live depressed, defeated, guilty, condemned, ashamed or unworthy. You were created to be victorious. Once again, Kaye's written a book that I know I will read again and again over the years. In fact, each book in the series fits that description. I can't wait for the saga to continue with Marz's story in Hard to Come By - I'm hoping to be able to add it to my list of keepers! PS - Here's my favorite of Jeremy's dirty t-shirts from this installment: It had the words, "The Man," with an arrow pointing upward, followed by, "The Legend," with an arrow pointing downward. Some Particulars HEA? Yes with Jenna and Easy, but the series plot is far from over! Love Triangle? Nope Cheating? Nope Explicit Sex? Yes Steam Rating: 3 out of 5 Consent? Crystal clear Trigger Warning? Warning for PTSD and suicidal thoughts.

This book.. I have mixed feelings. I would give it 5 stars, as it feels like coming home to an old friend. The prose is delightfully written - true Harper Lee. However, I have reservations about the ending which knocked off a star for me. While it is interesting to see what has happened to Scout in the time between To Kill A Mockingbird and now, it is just as great to see what kind of person she has become. I loved the stories of her childhood - the little insights into the intervening time - but I also loved reading about how Jean Louise Finch is as a person now. She is every bit as tough and free thinking as she appeared as a child. She struggles to be a 'lady' and find that balance of being true to herself and conforming to social norms. I got such a strong feeling of her continuing to be a feminist heroine. Then there is Atticus. The thing I dreaded most was changing my views on Atticus, but it is essential. We read Mockingbird through a child's eyes (or a nostalgic narrator looking back through her childhood viewpoint) and so Atticus is a virtually flawless human being. He is a hero. To have our view of him changed is one of the points of this book. Scout must learn that her father is human and flawed as part of her growing up process and we too must realise that even the most virtuous of people have their flaws. The issue of race is explored very strongly, with a great deal of racist thought and language present. Jean Louise represents us, with her colour-blind view and ideas of equality regardless of race. It is through our modern view that we feel the outrage at the behaviour of Maycomb. There are shades of grey within the novel - degrees of racist thought and reasoning behind various views. I was left feeling somewhat dissatisfied by the ending. No spoilers, but I felt it to be a bit of a slap in the face and not fully resolved. Do read for yourself and share your thoughts, as it may affect everyone differently. It was worth the read and worth the wait though, just to see the characters again.

4.5 "Bossman" stars! Bossman by Vi Keeland is a sweet, sexy, fun, flirty read that has epic banter and a bit of angst. This book made me laugh, warmed my heart, made me swoon, and made me really feel for the characters. The wonderful writing, refreshing characters, and interesting plot made this a wonderful 2016 read! We meet Reese Annesley while she is on a dry, boring date. Trying to arrange an emergency exit plan, she encounters a hot guy named Chase Parker who ends up crashing her awful date during his own date. That one random encounter with Chase brings all sorts of funny to the table, literally, and at the end of the night, Reese is intrigued by Chase and can't stop thinking of him. Unfortunately there is little chance of bumping into him again in a city as big as NYC. Reese has worked for the same cosmetics company for the past seven years and after a mistake with a co-worker, she is left looking for a new job. Reese and Chase end up running into each other again and this interaction is just as hilarious as the first time they met. It leads to a job offer that she can't turn down. When Reese starts at Parker Industries, the company owned by Chase, her passion for the industry returns and she finds herself loving her job again. She doesn't want to do anything to jeopardize her job and Chase doesn't make it easy for her. "I'm attracted to you. Really attracted to you. Have been since the first time I saw you. Tried to be respectful, considering you were seeing someone. Done doing that. If you work here, I'm going to try to get you into my bed." Chase is smart, funny, loves what he does and is good at his job. When he puts his mind to something he is used to succeeding, so when his sight is set on Reese, he is determined to make Reese his. "Let me get this straight... you're sharing a meal twice a week, alone with him?" "That's right. In a non-dating capacity." "Which means what? You won't be fucking at the end of the night?" I sipped my drink. "Exactly." Jules cracked up. "He talked you into this crap?" "What do you mean?" "You're dating him and don't even know it. I might love this man." I wasn't dating him. Was I? We were just sharing a meal twice a week. Getting to know each other. Not seeing other people. And thinking of each other while we took care of ourselves. OMG. I am dating him! Though Reese and Chase have amazing chemistry and the sexual tension is thick from the start, it's a slow build to an actual relationship. When they finally decide to take a chance on each other, they can't keep their hands off of each other and it is HOT! So is Chase's dirty mouth! My eyes closed. "Chase..." He buried his face in my hair from behind, inhaling deeply, then wrapped it around his hand and tugged my head back. "You're soaked. How long will you stay mad at me for bending you over this desk and fucking you, Buttercup?" "We shouldn't." "Your mouth says no, but your body is screaming yes." Bossman is a fantastic read. I loved the plot and the execution of the forbidden romance element. I liked the direction the story took and thought it was believable. Reese and Chase were perfect for each other. Their relationship both in the bedroom and out of it was wonderful and totally realistic. You could see their attraction from the start and it only compounded until they couldn't keep their hands off each other. The banter between the two of them was hilarious and I found myself laughing out loud numerous times. The sexual tension was well written and the slow buildup lead to some majorly steamy sexy time. Chase is a fantastic character and I loved him. He is charming, sexy, confident and totally swoon worthy. I loved everything about him from his sweet words to his dirty mouth. I loved that Chase made it crystal clear that he was interested in Reese and that there was no one else on his mind. I loved his determination as well as his patience as he pursued Reese. He was a complex character that had a tragic past and my heart broke for him when everything is revealed. I didn't fault him for his actions when he pushed Reese away and I am glad he finally realized what he was missing. "Don't ask me to explain it, but when I'm around you, I'm happy. That's all I'm after." Reese was wonderful. She lives with a fear but she doesn't let it pull her down. She is sweet, beautiful, funny, and caring. I completely understood her reluctance to start a relationship with a co-worker, her boss's boss no less, and with the unhealthy relationship her parents had, I know it was difficult for her to look into the future and fully imagine what she and Chase could have. She was mature about her relationship and I loved that when she decided to take the step with Chase she went all in. I was the balance to his unsteadiness. He was the courage to my fear. I loved this book and the sweet epilogue that left a smile on my face. If you haven't met Chase yet, you really need to read Bossman. It is fantastic in every way!

So I'm checking out Comixology's new all-you-can-eat subscription service, and I figure the first series I should try is The Walking Dead. I've been wanting to read it for a while, but there are so many damn volumes that I've never gotten around to it. Now I have no excuse. Okay, so it's a zombie story, very straightforward, but done with a dynamic art style. And the characterization is good ... as long as we're talking about male characters. After one volume, none of the women have been allowed to do anything but wash laundry, gripe about their lives, and practice target shooting -- which does absolutely no good, because as soon as a zombie shows up, they're reduced to incoherent screaming while the men swing into action and save the day. The fact that this passes the Bechdel test is mainly down to the women having a conversation about laundry detergent. I shit you not. Meanwhile, we get plenty of conversations between the male characters about the women, which mainly come down to what a bitch the various female characters are. Which is entirely fair within the storyverse because that's all the writer ever lets them be. Even the protagonist's wife is portrayed that way due to her constantly second guessing the hero. It doesn't matter whether she's right, such as the time she warns her husband not to go into the city -- when he barely escapes getting bitten, he tells his companion not to mention it to his wife, because that would just make her more bitchy -- or wrong, like when she objects to her seven year old son learning to use a gun, only for him to save her life a couple pages later by taking out a zombie that was about to eat her. (She of course dropped her gun in panic. 'Cause women, right?) I know this is a series for guys, but come on! This is the story of a zombie apocalypse. Any woman who manages to survive should be bad ass and capable of looking after herself. Not a freaking laundress who's incapable of contributing anything to the party beyond nagging.

This book gave me mixed feelings. On one hand, it was full of action, plot twists in every corner and there were a lot of things happening all the time, so it was not a boring book. On the other hand, a lot of the characters I loved from the first book begin to change, some for the better some for worse. By the second half of the book you just get paranoid... no one is to be trusted anymore because everyone seems to have a secret agenda and you can clearly see that it's not just you who doesn't really trust the characters but they don't trust each other either, which is like the root of all the problems they're having and I just wanted to scream at them. I loved Tobias in the first book and I loved the romance between him and Tris. But in this second installment, they fight non-stop and never seem to agree on anything, so I felt like I had to pick sides and I found myself pulling towards Tris, even though she wasn't at her best either. After the second half of the book and maybe even before that I practically lost all my love for Tobias: he was being so blind, unreasonable and stubborn that he spend all his time criticizing everything Tris was doing and was unwilling to hear her explanations. This whole change in Tobias behavior and the relationship between the main characters disappointed me to the point that I fell on a reading slump for almost a month, because I refused to start another book without finishing this one, but at the same time I just didn't care enough for the characters to keep reading. I had to force myself to read the second half and I got little to no reward for it until the very end, because things stayed the same way until literally the last chapter. To be fair, I have to add that part of what made me so reluctant to keep going with this book was the fact that I caught a mayor spoiler about the ending of Allegiant (the third and final book on this trilogy). Either way, I was about two weeks into my reading slump when I found out about this spoiler so I guess both factors are to be considered here. If I set apart the drama with the characters and focus only on the world-building and where the story is going plot-wise, I think this book is even more interesting than the first one. The world keeps building on itself and every time a secret is revealed you're like one step farther from the truth. Which I know sounds ridiculous, but when/if you read this book, you see that the mysteries keep piling one on top of the other, making the world much more intricate and fantastic. I don't know yet if I'll read Allegiant. I thought I wouldn't since I couldn't even finish this one before, but the freaking cliffhanger ending is making me doubt my decision. So, I guess we'll see.

I can't fault Hillbilly Elegy for lack of ambition - even at age 31, writing your memoirs and then extrapolating from you own experience to draw conclusions about the environment you grew up in is no joke. But I can and will fault it for its surface-level approach and lazy prose. I actually think this book would have benefited hugely from a narrower scope - either stick to the memoir passages and expand them to include incidents that maybe don't have an obvious object lesson to draw; or stick to the sociological study of Appalachia that makes up the book's other half, roughly. Trying to do both in well under 300 pages means that everything feels rushed and disorganized. There are mixed metaphors and cliches on every page - after another incident with his mother promising to get her life together, Vance observes, "but the road to hell is paved with good intentions," with all the gravity of someone coming up with that analogy for the first time. To me, that's something an editor should have caught - this book could easily have been tighter and more cohesive with a few judicious edits and some reorganizing. I also feel duty-bound to let you know I listened to the audiobook and it was... not great. Vance reads it himself and I realize that's common practice with memoirs, but it was maybe not the best choice here.

Chase, the main character and his older brother Noah get into the writer Camus on summer because of their neighbor Melinda. Both start quoting it reguarly throughout the book. While Invincible Summer definately did grab my interest i couldnt find myself to absoluely adore this book. I enjoyed reading it and connected very well to the main character Chase, but something about this book wasn't enough for me. I can't say much without revealing any spoilers so I won't. What i will tell you is that if your in the search for a book that deals with heavy topics and family tragedies this one's for you.

This is the kind of book that I call "mind fodder": quick, fun reads that ultimately aren't all that great but are enjoyable and give your brain a break from having to think too hard. I'll tell you now, I think this was the fourth time that I have read this book, so this is a review coming from someone who knows the plot quite well and also knows what happens in later books (except for The Crown, hence the reason I re-read this). When I first read The Selection series I absolutely adored it. I saw the cover and thought it would be fluffy nonsense but my friends convinced me to give it a try and I loved it. Now, it being a few years later, and I having read more (and much better) books I now realise that it is only a bit above fluffy nonsense, but above it all the same. I loved it enough still to be quite disappointed in Kiera Cass and involved people when I found out about the controversy that happened around this book a few years ago. While The Selection is a fun read that gives you the feels, it doesn't have much else going for it. The base line for its plot is rather unoriginal, there is only the bare necessities of world building, it has a slight slut-shaming case, America isn't the most fun protagonist to read about (and she gets worse in the next book), and it has the dreaded love triangle (that gets worse too). Do not go into this book expecting much, that way you won't be too disappointed. If you read this and couldn't stand the last few chapters, then either don't continue on with the series or skim it until you get to The One, which if I remember correctly lays off the love triangle sub-plot a bit. It also gets a bit more into the history and politics in the later books which is nice. Again, I recommend this book when you want something light to read which will give your brain a rest. If you are looking for a brilliant novel, with complex characters and story line, then look elsewhere.

This one worms around you, subtly, until you find yourself glued to the story, always wanting to know what happens next. Mandel does a fantastic job of weaving the post-apocalyptic and pre-apocalyptic worlds together in a series of flashbacks and through characters that flirt across the pages and come together in a few things: the Station Eleven comics, the Travelling Symphony, and the airport. The story follows Kristen and Arthur, who in the pre-apocalyptic world are actors in a production of King Lear. From there, the novel spins off to follows Arthur's life pre-apocalypse, and all of the wonderful characters that fill his world - Clark, his gay best friend; Miranda, the first of his ex-wives; and Elizabeth, the second, whom he falls in love with at a dinner party. Post-apocalypse, the story traces Kristen's journey with a roving Shakespearian band of actors and musicians through a world marked by the absence of people. It's a wonderful, engaging read, and one of the best books I've read in a weeks.

Girl of Nightmares takes place 6 months after Anna Dressed in Blood. Cas is trying to move on with his life... unsuccessfully. He's tormented by visions of Anna being tortured by something unseen. They can't communicate with each other so he doesn't know where she is or what is going on, only that she is being beaten, burned, and broken. Both Carmel and Thomas tell him he has to let her go, but it's not that easy. After a few close misses while hunting for ghosts, that jeopardize not only him, but his best friends, he's determined to find out the answers and do what he can to save Anna. In Girl of Nightmares we get all the answers we were still looking for at the end of Anna Dressed in Blood. Plus, we get some wonderful character development. At the end of book 1 I'll admit, I only liked Cas... but at the end of Girl of Nightmares, I loved him. I understood his obsession with Anna and I wanted him to find a solution, a way that he could help her and still be happy. He is snarky and funny and even though he hasn't had friends growing up, he cherishes the friends he's made. And Thomas, he's adorable and sweet and I wanted to hug the poor kid. We also got to know a bit more about Carmel, and I loved how strong she ended up being... although at one point I stated "I wanted to punch her in the babymaker." I did understand her situation and where she was coming from. I mean, I saw it coming, but it angered me, I can't lie. What I really loved about this book though, was Blake's ability to take this ghost story and turn it into something more. I mean Anna, this evil ghost sacrificed herself for Cas (& Thomas & Carmel) in book 1 and his hope for her to find peace is crushed with these visions he has of her. While Blake definitely had the creepy scenes (The Suicide Forest and the Creepy Dead Grandma thing), there is also witty dialogue and some very lighthearted moments too. What makes this book though, is the ending that Blake gave us. I spend the last 4-5 chapters of this book trying to predict how it would end... I won't spoil it here, you'll just have to read it, but I'm incredibly satisfied with it and I wasn't expecting it in the least. If you haven't read Anna Dressed in Blood - go do that first, then come read the second (and final) book in the series. I think you'll love it! This review can be found on my blog, Fic Fare:

I'm really confused about what I can write and what I can't write here on Goodreads. One of my recent reviews was deleted for being not about the book. Your review of Logic: A Very Short Introduction was recently flagged by Goodreads members as potentially off-topic. As the review is not about the book, it has been removed from the site. I can't complain about that, they were quite right - I had actually shelved that book on my TO READ site, so by definition, I hadn't read it yet. So the logic is, I think, that ANY remark about a book you haven't read yet is "potentially off-topic". This means that ANY comments you have made about a book on your TO READ shelves should be deleted by the unhappy staff members who are tasked with zapping this stuff. (Do they read George Orwell essays in their lunch breaks? I would like to think so.) They don't need to wait for the non-review to be flagged, they can just go ahead and zap any review they find on anyone's TO READ shelf. But, you know, they aren't doing that... so far. Well, not to me, anyway. So until we get a little more clarity about this, I would like to present a short entertainment which I freely admit cannot possibly be a review of Tampa because I haven't read it yet, and therefore is "potentially off-topic". Okay, enough with the mealymouth, I'll make it simple : it's COMPLETELY off-topic. There you go, I'm trying to help here. HOW TO CHOOSE YOUR NEXT NOVEL When I'm three quarters through my current novel I get the urge to pick the next one. It's a horrible urge - next, next, next. O the disease of novel-reading - one ailment I hope I'm never cured of. So anyway, which one to choose out of the dozens on the groaning shelf? The one with the sexiest cover? The one with the waggly tail? No, that's how you choose which dog to buy. How about the serious one which has been sitting glowering at me for about a decade and which will make me a better person? So I thought I'd approach the problem scientifically this time, and base my decision on First Lines. I mean, if I was a novelist, I'd want to spear the reader like a fish with a really strong first line. So I'm the fish, spear me. Here are ten contenders, taken from the groaning shelf at random. 1) Tampa by Alissa Nutting I spent the night before my first day of teaching in an excited loop of hushed masturbation on my side of the mattress, never falling asleep. Wow, like not sleeping for the whole night? Wouldn't you be totally zombified on your first day at the new job? Anyway, yeah, I want to know what kind of nutcase we're dealing with here, so I'm hooked. 2) Platform by Michel Houellebecq Father died last year. Oh that's so tiny I will allow him another sentence. I don't subscribe to the theory by which we only become truly adult when our parents die; we never become truly adult. Mmm, so so. I can't say I'm bothered one way or the other. 3) The Lowland by Jhumpa Lahri East of the Tolly Club, after Deshapran Sashmal Road splits in two, there is a small mosque. I read a book about literary devices and one chapter was about first lines of novels and the guy was saying that you really need a strong first line, obviously, and he was reeling off all these great ones, you know, Call me Fishmeal and The clocks were striking 13 and all of those. Well, it seems most novelists do not subscribe to this idea at all and are happy to write very dull first sentences. 4) The Mosquito Coast by Paul Theroux We drove past Tiny Polski's mansion house to the main road, and then the five miles into Northampton, Father talking the whole way about savages and the awfulness of America - how it got turned into a dope-taking, door-locking, ulcerated danger-zone of rabid scavengers and criminal millionaires and moral sneaks. Yes, that's more like it. I'm interested. Let's go. 5) Continental Drift by Russell Banks It's not memory you need for telling this story, the sad story of Robert Raymond Dubois, the story that ends along the back streets and alleys of Miami, Florida, on a February morning in 1981... Hold on there, Russell ! I finally found a full stop towards the end of page one, it's one of those clausally incontinent whoppers. But yeah, I like that. 6) Burr by Gore Vidal Shortly before midnight, July 1, 1833, Colonel Aaron Burr, aged seventy-seven, married Eliza Jumel, born Bowen fifty-eight years ago (more likely sixty-five but remember : she is prone to litigation! Well, this is lighthearted enough. He's trying to put me at ease - this will be history with its tie loosened. Gets its jauntiness in immediately. Nice. 7) A Fire Upon the Deep by Vernor Vinge How to explain? How to describe? Even the omniscient viewpoint quails. Oh deario. This is a much-praised space-opera but is that not one of the clunkient, least appetising first lines you've ever seen? Quails? Who says quails? is this going to be a novel where they use verily and quoth? Back on the shelf. 0 out of 10. 8) Omensetter's Luck by William H Gass Now folks today we're going to auction off Missuss Pimber's things. I love this, I instantly want to read on. There's no quotation marks, this being The Gassman, a notorious modernist, so I'm expecting it to be all streamily conscious and that. 9) Crystal Vision by Gilbert Sorrentino I will call this drink the Flowers of Summer, the Magician says, I would call a drink the Flowers of Summer too, but I hate magicians. 10) Blonde by Joyce Carol Oates There came Death hurtling along the Boulevard in waning sepia light. Ooh, that's a bit pulpy and lurid. It's not all going to be like that is it? This is supposed to be about Marilyn Monroe, and she did die. Must be one of those stories that start at the end and then flashback (for 738 pages). So, we have a winner. Alissa, it's you, you saucy minx. This makes me very sad. I was so invested in this series. I liked Shiver, loved Linger. And absolutely hated the ending of Forever. Grace has started shifting. In the months without her Sam barely lives. They have to find out a cure that makes sure they will be able to be together, forever. Starting these novels, you know they aren't going to be action-packed. They're romance books of the dreamy kind. You float through them on a happy cloud of beautiful descriptions. Ms Stiefvater is a very talented writer, and her language is amazing. Sadly, Forever fell flat for me. It was as if every bit of spirit was sucked out of the main characters. Dreamy Sam turns into whiny Sam. Independant Grace turns into numb Grace. They just mope around, feel bad for themselves and do absolutely nothing about it. Not even Grace who is such a do-person instead of a thinker. Cole and Isabel are a great couple, but there was way too little of them in the book. I wanted more chemistry, but instead there were more fights. I'm one of those people that can't just abandon a series mid-way. I stick with the characters to the end. I want to know where they end up, and with who. I want to know who lives and who dies. Doesn't matter how long it takes, I like to have the closure of a series ending. I will not spoil it for you, but Forever ends on a big droopy cliffhanger. It ends with someone maybe or maybe not dying. That my friends, is not what I call closure. That isn't even what I call an ending for "open interpretation". That just damn sucky. I wish I liked Forever better, I really do. It ruins the series for me now. Not feeling like rereading Shiver any time soon, to be disappointed by this book all over again.

A friend of mine recommended Katie MacAlister. She said I should try one of her books if I want something fun to read. And I did have a great time reading this It's All Greek to Me. It was pretty light and no dull/dark moments in the book. Actually, I don't think there is a real mystery or even a story line: girl arrives in a foreign place, meets a rich-handsome-guy, falls head over heels and lives HEA. Yes, there are a lot of steamy scenes. Nevertheless, I found the book utterly refreshing. The usual chase between the male and female leads in nonexistent. There was no beating around the bush. Both of them took the plunge. Which somehow I am thankful for, because really, the characters are strong-minded people who know exactly what they want to do with their lives. You will eventually be together, so why waste time? Was there a conflict? Yes, there were tiny conflicts - no melodramas at all. This fact will probably frustrate some of the readers. I like Harry (although I find her real name weird). She is one of the most pragmatic ladies I have met in fiction-land. She's feisty, witty and sarcasm is probably part of her accent. She's strong, and doesn't lose her mind when the two of them fights or has a misunderstanding. Harry's inability to remember Iakovos Papaioannou's name (which I even could not recall easily) is an additional entertainment. Her ingenious versions are really amusing. They settle their conflicts as soon as it arises and move on to the next. She's very vocal about her emotions, tells him that she loves him, but he won't tell her just the same (although it is pretty much obvious). It's really cute how she would try to goad him in speaking the three little words - and you would never guess where, how, and when did he said 'I love you' to her - it was just freaking hilarious. The secondary characters like Theo adds spice to the story and I sincerely hope Katie MacAlister would write his happy ending too. For future readers, I advise you not to expect too much from this book. It is good, you will have fun reading it but it may not have the depth that you would like in a novel. However, if you want a fun, light read in between those heavy doses of romantic novels - I suggest you give It's All Greek to Me a chance and you'll just not stop laughing your hearts out.

Is it so arrogant to want something that doesn't change with the wind? That doesn't crumble at the first sign of adversity? The Wrath and the Dawn is a debut novel and is a retelling of the tale of A Thousand and One Nights. I expected a lot from this book, and while some of my expectations were met, it just let me down in other sections. This book could've been a 5 star book if it had been more developed. The Wrath and the Dawn follows a girl named Shahrzad, who volunteers to marry the boy-king. Khalid, the boy-king, takes a bride each day, and at every dawn, she is killed. Shahrzad's motivation lies with the fact that her best friend was killed at the king's hands, and she wants to avenge her friend's death. Shahrzad does something no one else has: she survives the first night. As she gets to know the king, she realizes he might not be the monster everyone believes him to be. She must reconcile the two side of her--the one that has feelings for him and the side that remains loyal to her friend. Love is a force unto itself, sayyidi. For love, people consider the unthinkable... and often achieve the impossible. I would not sneer at its power. The Things I Liked - The romance was utterly breathtaking. I was swooning. There is so much development of the relationship between Khalid and Shahrzad. I am completely rooting for them. How could you possibly not like this? "What are you doing to me, you plague of a girl?" he whispered. "If I'm a plague, then you should keep your distance, unless you plan on being destroyed." The weapons still in her grasp, she shoved against his chest. "No." His hands dropped to her waist. "Destroy me." - The writing is so detailed. It's like you could reach out and touch and taste everything in the world. It's an incredibly immersive experience. - Shahrzad, in general, is a quite likable main character. She's very witty and doesn't hesitate to defend herself. She isn't helpless. More than that, she takes what she knows, puts it to a test, and changes her opinions based on what she learns. - Khalid stunned me with his depth as a character. He has this huge back story, and he is so complicated. The best part? He is nothing that he seems to be. Khalid develops so perfectly, and I applaud the author for his transformation. - The world within the castle was fascinating. I loved seeing the interactions between the soldiers, servants, etc. Everything within the palace felt real. I believed and cared about the conflicts. The Things I Disliked - There are random words inserted into the book that are in a different language. I know this is an attempt to further place me inside the world, but it had the opposite effect. Most of the time, I simply skipped over the words I didn't understand. I should mention that there is a glossary in the back, but I didn't feel like spending the time flipping back and forth. - This book begins with the wedding day right away. There is zero development of the relationships between Shahrzad and her sister, her father, her friends, and Tariq, her childhood love. Due to this oversight on the author's part, I did not care about their struggles throughout the book. I didn't understand their viewpoints or the draw that they had toward each other, so every time a chapter from their perspective came, I inwardly groaned. I definitely preferred the world within the palace because it held more substance. - Magic plays a role in this novel, and it isn't explained. I don't know what it can do or where it comes from. I'm hoping that the next book offers more of an explanation. - There is a possible love triangle on the horizon between Shahrzad, Khalid, and Tariq. Let this be known: I dislike Tariq with everything that I have. It might be due to his lack of development, or maybe it's just because I don't like his bullheadedness. He listens to nobody, and his number on an aggravation scale is a 10 out of 10. - Lastly, the ending left something to be desired. I'm quite confused too, but I will be reading the next one, if only because I'd like to see some more beautiful romance between the two characters that I adore.

This was one of my very favorite books as a child, but not because of the colors or the caterpillar--it was because of the food! I've had a slight obsession with food even as a youngling, and the movies and books I remember best are the ones that were about food, or had a scene to do with food. In any event, the Very Hungry Caterpillar remains a classic, and for good reason. It is colorful and creative, with varying-size pages, and provides a lot of interest for young readers. It helps them learn their days of the week and how to count, and also gives you a gentle nudge about eating healthy, especially while growing up. All the candy and junk the caterpillar eats on Saturday, which a caterpillar (or little boy or girl) shouldn't be eating, gives him a stomach ache. He feels much better when he eats a leafy green. There are so many good parts to this book, and it's so endearing that you can't help but want to read it to your own younglings.

Before I even begin this review, let it be known that I'm rating this book on what was presented and not for the potential it had. Leonie Woodville is a 17 year old college student who had a rather reclusive life with her father, she is deemed anti-social from the start and as such is awkward as well as abrasive. Unbeknownst to her she is a CHOSEN, an individual with abilities of the elements. Except she's special she is the last PULSAR - a fire elemental. While Leonie didn't have a fantastic upbringing or an ideal life - as a rather horrible incident occurs - she is a rather unlikable character from the get go. Snappy, abrasive, overly snarky and fairly mean. We're not meant to forget that she is anti-social, however when KORREN comes onto the seen it seems that isn't so... Korren is an immortal being, a Kytaen which is essentially a creature that is able to take on a humanoid form, they are the protectors of their chosen or what is known as their Keeper to them. Korren has witnessed a lot in his years and has waited 200 years to be uncaged. He is angsty, bitter and distrusfful of everyone for just reason. He's a brooding sort who glares from across the way and doesn't seem likable either, but when you compare him to Leonie he's a ray of sunshine. As far as the plot goes, it's fairly interesting. The last Pulsar is brought back to her "home" and is revered, but her return brings a fair amount of trouble as well, as rebels congregate and plot to take her down or rather unleash her and use her for their own devices. Meanwhile, Korren, Leonie's protector finds himself battling with whether or not he wants to protect her - he really is just looking out for himself. Sounds great, right? Well, it had oodles of potential, but the writing quality just wasn't there. A lot of the times it read like an angsty teen girls diary. I almost DNF @ 30%, but I held out because there were times it seemed promising. However, there were then moments that read like this. "Light Magic?" "The essence of magic." "Oh" "Do you mind?" "No." There are pages where this is all that it consists of. A lot of dialogue that is short, or it will go to the next extreme and be overly informative. There has to be a balance and because of this the reader doesn't get to witness a lot of what actually happens in the world the author is trying to create. What I would ask Simlett is, "What do you want us to feel and what would you like us to walk away with after reading?" because after reading this I'm no wiser than what I was when I began reading, I'm definitely frustrated because I felt like it was just drawn out for the second book - yes it does make you want to read it, if you can look past the imperfections and the room for improvement. So, while I give this book a 1, it had a grand amount of potential and I see that. I see that in the writer, too. ~Blog~Instagram~

I remember the first time I read Mockingjay I was frustrated with how frequently I felt like I couldn't really picture what was happening, action-wise, or didn't think the locations and setting were described adequately; especially when Katniss and her team are making their way through the Capitol. I was, therefore, pleasantly surprised when I finally watched the movie and saw that what was depicted on-screen was very close to what I had pictured in my mind. Compared to the first two books, there really isn't much action, at least not of the same caliber as the Games. When Katniss does venture out into "battle," she gets injured, blacks out or is sedated, wakes up in the hospital, recovers and does that all over again. The strongest component of this book, in my opinion, is the emotional journeys of the characters. Spending more time on characters than battle tactics allowed Collins to gradually bring them to a place that felt right by the end of the book, it wasn't rushed or nonsensical--not a fairy-tale happy ending, but a very satisfying and truthful one.

First impressions: YOU GUYS. LADY NUN ASSASSINS. Enough said. Lasting impressions: Ismae may be one of my favorite heroines of all time. She's up there with Claire Randall, vying for the top spot. She's smart, humble, kind, merciful, and oh yeah - a stealthy handmaiden of death. Conflicting impressions: While the convent was a large focus of the first part of this book, the ending didn't tie up many loose ends in that regard. I have a feeling much of this information will become the focus in later books, but I felt a little jilted in this book when it came to Sybella and some of the other sisters. Overall impressions: It's a historical novel with courtly intrigue and a protagonist who is a kick-ass murderer. But a nice kick-ass murderer. I would have bet anyone a million dollars that I would love this book. Guess what? I win! The premise of this book could never hold the weight of its own ambition without a heroine that makes the reader care about her. From the very first page, Ismae stole my heart. Trapped under an abusive father, marked by Death himself to be an outcast, and thrust into a marriage with a disgusting pig of a man, I couldn't help but want something more for her. When she is offered a home and a purpose for her miserable life at St. Mortain's convent, Ismae can finally start to believe in herself. The bulk of the novel focuses on one of Ismae's first major assignments. She is assigned to play mistress to Lord Duval and accompany him to the Breton court to ferret out traitors that need assassinating. There is a delectable romance that builds between the two unlikely lovebirds, and I appreciated that LaFevers devoted more time to personality based obstacles than class driven ones. Yes he's a Lord and one of the most influential men at court, and she's just the lowly peasant girl, but that never seems to be the focus for why these two shouldn't fall in love. Perhaps why I loved Ismae so much was precisely because LaFevers made her more complicated than the usual historical trope. Despite her training and occupation, Ismae is an Everywoman. She's unsure of herself and makes mistakes. She follows at times she should be leading. She trusts when she shouldn't. Yet we don't fault her for any of it. We understand why she makes the decisions she does, and it makes her all the more believable and compelling. Do I think this story needed to meander through nearly 600 pages? No. There were moments where the pacing lagged and Ismae got a bit repetitive with her musings. At its core, however, this novel has a pure soul that guides us carefully through morally complicated situations that at times benefited from a lengthier examination. As Ismae determines her true calling as Death's handmaiden, the book culminates in one of the most spiritually enlightened moments I've ever experienced in fiction. The vast depth to this book offers pure pleasure to the reader. If you're willing to invest the time, it will heap its rewards upon you. There's a reason for the hype, and this one definitely lives up to it.
Will pick back up later.

Wow, that went south in a hurry. There are some books that should never be sequels, and this one is a good example. The plot is basically "Dearly, Departed goes on". There is no significant movement. Several more viewpoint characters are added and while they do have some good points, most of them sound the same. It was hard to get motivated to read several hundred more pages about a civil rights movement where I don't even understand the stakes. So this book is done. Luckily the author is moving on to other projects. Hopefully the next one will be as enjoyable as her debut. Memo to me: Sequels need to have a plot unique to them that still ties into the larger series story line. If there isn't a bad guy/ticking clock/problem that is unique to that novel then the sequel won't work.

A book with a very immature hero. I get he had a troubled past, and I get why he got into drugs and alcohol, and I get why he was so angry and broody. I've read multiple books with a hero and a bad past and a bad attitude, and I've had no problem with them. But this boy did not act like a kid with tortured past. He was just straight up immature. I know he was only 16 years old, and I guess in reality that's how immature 16 year old act, but it's a turn off for me. There wasn't a moment in the story where I was even remotely attracted to him.

A great read for the annual "Adopt an Emo" Week, if your school has one. Otherwise... Of course, I come to this book as someone whose first suicide attempt was at eight years old, and who spent roughly the next twenty years in varying states of contemplating 'self-murder.' Reading over some other reviews, it seems to me that it's people like me who take the greatest offense at this book, and the people who adore this book adore it for tackling a terribly important subject, in a terribly important way. I was not particularly offended, just disappointed. I had been hoping for something like a lengthy suicide note written from one deeply depressed teen to a friend, the only person she felt she owed an explanation to. Twilight-teen myopic, but sad and-- sincere. What I got was an angry, manipulative chain letter from beyond the grave to all the people who 'forced' her to commit suicide, or who 'could have saved her.' (Logistical issue I had with the book: I actually don't know anyone my age who has a working cassette player. I wonder at the absence of problems getting the cassettes to play on long-unused cassette players-- which fail if they get dirty or fall into long disuse. This would throw a wrench into Hannah's lovely little, "And the person who breaks this chain will be visited by my ghostly vengeance!") Honestly, part of the problem with this book might be the fact that the author is male. And the book describes the way (typically) that MEN commit suicide-- angrily, suddenly, vengefully-- not leaving long-planned, elaborate and convoluted bread crumb trails behind them. Women tend to suffer long depressions, long retreats from other people and from hope, dabbling with things like cutting or eating disorders for months or years. They attempt and attempt, and finally die accidentally on purpose. Hannah is not severely depressed. She is not mentally ill. She does not suffer severe bullying, because many people in school are friendly acquaintances, and no one lifts a hand against her. She does not have voices in her head telling her to kill herself. There are few feelings as intense as the shame and despair of an awkward teenage girl, but while Asher has undoubtedly done his research, he does not sound, even for a moment, like the typical suicidal teenage girl. But this is also not the typical female revenge suicide. For someone angry enough to insist that 13 specific people should have helped her, she is (in a very un-teenagerly fashion) intent on seeing the good points in her targets and not ranting. A lot of what Hannah wants with this attention-mongering, post-mortem scavenger hunt, could be achieved by a public-ish suicide 'attempt.' What she wanted to do was shine a light on herself and her suffering, and smear the people she wanted to smear. (My lack of sympathy comes from the fact that I have known people like this, who make demands of their loved ones or the world by holding themselves hostage. It's histrionic and absurd. But so is a lot of high school.) So why kill herself? Exactly NONE of her anger is self-directed. She could get all the lovely hand-wringing she wants from Clay and the others by faking her own death, or 'attempting' suicide. I suppose we're to think of Hannah as perfectly earnest and honest, perfectly objective in her narration, but that's hard for me to do since she's trying to pull strings from beyond the grave. If all she wanted was to have the truth of her death known-- she should have just left a note-- to a sympathetic ear, not the people she blames. She wants 13 people to feel bad about what they should have done, and is naive enough to trust that none of them will roll their eyes at her and get defensive. For me, in real life, her choice of 'suicide note' would rule her out as a purely reliable source of objectivity. Another issue with the book: it attempts to be about Everyteen. Because of the book's concept, it can't really help that, and yet it tells the story of a highly unusual suicide as if that were normative. While it is never mentioned, Hannah is obviously from a small town, and big city kids like me, from big city high schools 2000+ students strong-- are going to have a little trouble relating. For example, when I was a freshman a rumor went around that I was a prostitute. For the rest of my high school career, the occasional blowhard would ask me how much I cost. And you know what? I genuinely never cared. At all. Not even a little. In a big school, there are always people who haven't heard/haven't believed every rumor. I was suicidal for other reasons, reasons that never had anything to do with other people. Also, there were magnet schools that one could go to if the main school wasn't working out for you. I thought a lot of Hannah's problems could be solved by switching schools. Or, less ideally, running away from home, or, less ideally still, bringing a gun to school and firing on the kids she hates so much. She 'gives up' but she never feels the pull of the six-foot hole, never hears the window ledge calling her name. Others have talked at length about how jarring and dissonant the two narrative voices are, and how confusing it makes the story. All I can say is: I listened to this on audio with two different narrators, and I STILL had a hard time parsing out who was supposed to be who, at least at the beginning. Despite all this, I would have given the book three stars-- for the readable and unusual storytelling style-- if not for the ending, which was so painfully heavy-handed and moralistic it made me gag. Does anyone actually believe that depressed people are stupid enough not to realize when they've been made someone's 'project'? The story was clearly about one particular, unusual suicide, that forced me to suspend a LOT of disbelief, but I didn't mind too much because hey, mysteries are about one particular murder... but then I banged my shin on the soapbox at the end.
